ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
M. Zaeem Zulfiqar
Versus
The State and another.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties
order/ order/ or counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
28.04.2026 Mr. Asif Ali Tamboli, Advocate for the petitioner.
Mr. Usman Rasool Ghumman, AAG.
Rao Abdul Raheem, Advocate for complainant /
respondent No.2.
Asif Nawaz, D.D, NCCIA, ICT.
MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI J. Through
the instant criminal miscellaneous, the
petitioner has prayed for his post arrest bail in
case F.I.R No.52/24, dated 13.02.2024, under
Section 11 of PECA, 2016 read with Sections
295-A, 295-B, 295-C, 298-A & 109 PPC, P.S
F.I.A Cyber Crime Circle, Islamabad.
2. Brief facts referred in the instant FIR
lodged on the complaint of Muhammad Mansoor
Khan are that one person namely M. Tanveer
with criminal intent and ulterior motive illegally
and un-authorizedly created/developed and
further uploaded/transmitted/disseminated as
well as projected/displayed blasphemous
contents i.e. images, pictures in respect of the
Almighty Allah, The Holy Prophet P.B.U.H, The
Holy Quran alongwith sacrilegious, loathsome
narration/speech and text on private part of the
2
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
naked human body using WhatsApp accounts
and profiles. Hence, this FIR.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner
contends that this is the second post-arrest bail
application of the petitioner and his earlier post-
arrest bail application was dismissed vide order
dated 11.02.2025, passed in Crl.Misc. No.2260-B
of 2024, wherein a direction was issued to the
learned Trial Court seized with the matter to
conclude the trial within a period of eight
months. However, despite the said direction, the
trial has not yet been concluded and the
petitioner is behind the bars since 23.02.2024
and statutory period has already been over as
provided in the relevant offences; therefore, he is
entitled to post-arrest bail till the conclusion of
the trial. It is further contended that delay is
attributable to the prosecution and that the role
of the petitioner in delay or conclusion of the
trial is not apparent from the record.
4. Conversely, learned Counsel for the
complainant has opposed the instant post-arrest
bail application on the ground that total 55
hearings have been conducted by the Trial
Court, whereas witnesses were present on 31
dates. However, despite the best efforts of the
complainant as well as the prosecution, only
3
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
seven witnesses out of 13 PWs have been
recorded and the delay is attributable to the
petitioner’s side.
5. Arguments heard, record perused.
6. The original order sheet reflects that the
petitioner was nominated in the above-
mentioned case on 13.02.2024 and he was
arrested on 23.02.2024, whereafter challan was
submitted in Court on 24.05.2024 and charge
was framed on 09.10.2024. The first post-arrest
bail application was dismissed on 11.02.2025
through Crl. Misc. No. 2260-B of 2024 on merits
with direction to the trial Court seized with the
matter to conclude the trial within a period of
eight months. However, till date only seven PWs
have been recorded and cross-examined out of
total 13 PWs. Both sides have further highlighted
that out of 55 dates of hearing, on 31 dates
witnesses were present before the trial Court, on
08 dates, prosecution witnesses were absent, on
06 occasions, Presiding Officer was not available,
and on 04 dates lawyers’ strike was observed.
7. Besides this aspect, this Court has also
observed that co-accused Hassan Abid had
earlier filed Crl.Misc. No.1044-B of 2024, which
was dismissed on 13.06.2024 with direction to
the trial Court seized with the matter to conclude
4
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
the trial within six months. Similarly, Hassan
Abid, again filed Crl.Misc.No.1607-B of 2025,
which was also dismissed on 10.10.2025 by this
Court with direction to the learned Trial Court
seized with the matter to conclude the trial
within a period of next two months. Therefore,
record reflects that number of directions have
been passed by this Court for conclusion of trial,
but the evidence could not be concluded. In this
regard, I have attended the order sheets of the
Trial Court, which reflect that the prosecutor of
FIA/NCCIA was not present in the trial Court nor
properly representing the prosecution, which has
caused serious impediment in the trial.
8. The record further reflects that the forensic
analysis report of the accused/petitioner
Muhammad Zaeem Zulfiqar was not submitted
before the Court, which was required to be
submitted through supplementary challan. In
this regard, a show cause notice was also issued
by the trial Court to the Investigating Officer for
non-submission of the report, as reflected from
order dated 09.10.2025, and this aspect is
continuously reflected in orders dated
10.10.2025, 16.10.2025, 18.10.2025,
25.10.2025, and 05.11.2025, and on some
occasions non-bailable warrants of arrest have
5
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
also been issued. However, no explanation has
been rendered by the prosecution side, as the
trial Court has made serious efforts by issuing
notices and even non-bailable warrants, but
despite best efforts, the forensic report has not
been submitted.
9. At this stage, learned Counsel for the
complainant side contends that the report has
been submitted in the Court and is available on
record; however, this assertion was belied by
order dated 11.12.2025, passed by trial Court,
wherein no such report was placed on record,
and this position continued in December,
January, and thereafter.
10. This Court also requisitioned a report from
the trial Court regarding the progress of the
case, wherein the trial Court highlighted multiple
factors reflecting delay in conclusion of trial,
which is as under:
On 10.10.2025, 06 PWs were present but
learned counsel for the accused were not
present, even otherwise, forensic report to the
extent of accused Muhammad Zaeem Zulfiqar
was also not received, therefore, case was
adjourned for 16.10.2025. On 16.10.2025,
18.10.2025, 25.10.2025 and 05.11.2025, the
proceedings of this case was adjourned on the
request of learned defence counsel as
supplementary report under section 173 Cr.P.C
to the extent of accused Muhammad Zaeem
Zulfiqar was not submitted.
On 18.12.2025, a show cause notice under
section 174/175 to the I.O for submission of
supplementary report regarding forensic report
to the extent of accused Muhammad Zaeem
6
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
Zulfiqar, however, till date no such report has
been received. On 06.01.2026 and 22.01.2026,
although PWs were present but learned
Prosecutor was not present, therefore, case
was adjourned. On 07.02.2026 no one present
on behalf of accused persons and proceedings
of the case was adjourned for 23.02.2026.
11. Considering all these aspects, it appears
that the apparent delay in conclusion of trial is
attributable to the prosecution side, and even
the learned trial Court has put serious effort, but
no justiciable reasons have been brought on
record as to why the Director General, FIA or
D.G NCCIA is unable to produce the prosecutor
or the forensic report with regard to the accused
M. Zaeem Zulfiqar. Such aspect outrightly
persuades this Court to grant post-arrest bail on
statutory delay in terms of the principle laid
down in 2024 SCMR 28 (Muhammad Usman
Vs. The State and another), wherein it has
been held that the right accrues when statutory
period is completed without fault on the part of
the accused person.
12. Similarly, while calculating the quantum of
delay attributable to an accused, the Court is
required to consider whether the progress and
conclusion of trial were delayed by any act or
omission of the accused. While ascertaining
delay, cumulative effect and disposal of the case
has to be considered and its assessment cannot
7
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
be determined mathematically by merely
excluding those dates for which adjournment
was sought by the accused. The main factor for
consideration is attendance of witnesses and
whether, despite the matter having become ripe
for evidence, delay was caused by the accused.
13. In this regard, reliance is placed upon
1983 SCMR 72 (Nazir Hussain Vs. Ziaul Haq
and others), PLD 1982 SC 424 (Akhtar Abbas
Vs. The State), PLD 1990 SC 934 (Moundar
and others Vs. The State), 1998 SCMR 897
(Abdur Rashid Vs. The State), PLD 1995 SC
49 (Zahid Hussain Shah Vs. The State), and
1998 PCRLJ [AJ&K] 358 (Muhammad
Sadeeque Vs. Muhammad Behram and
another), whereby bail on statutory grounds
under the third proviso has been recognized even
where the last witness has been recorded by the
Trial Court.
14. For what has been discussed above, instant
petition is ALLOWED and the petitioner is
admitted to post arrest bail subject to his
furnishing bail bonds in the sum of
Rs.200,000/- with one surety in the like amount
to the satisfaction of learned Trial Court.
8
Crl. Misc. No.379-B-2026
(MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI)
JUDGE
RAMZAN

case_title: Dr. Muhammad Aslam Khaki VS Chairman, Council of Islamic Ideology, Islamabad etc.
before: Honourable Mr. Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani
author: Honourable Mr. Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani
description: Petitioner states that NCCIA sought opinion of Council of Islamic Ideology for alleged remarks by an Engineer Ali Muhammad Mirza for which remarks FIR U/s 295C (FIR No. 563-2025 dated 26.08.2025 U/s 295-C PPC 11 PECA 2016 P.S. City Jhelum, District Jhelum, Punjab) has already been registered against him. The CCI has opined the remarks to be blasphemous. Challenges the opinion / FATWA of Council of Islamic Ideology.
discussed_laws: under Section 295-C PPC | under Articles 229 and 230 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973

JUDGMENT SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
W.P No.3972-2025
Dr. Muhammad Aslam Khaki
Versus
Council of Islamic Ideology through its Chairman and others.
Petitioner by: Dr. Muhammad Aslam Khaki,
Advocate in person, alongwith
Hafiz Muhammad Tahir and
Ammar Altaf Satti, Advocates.
Respondents by: Mr. Rashid Hafeez, Additional
Attorney General.
Date of Decision: 27.04.2026.
……………………………………………………………………………….
MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI J., Through this writ
petition, the petitioner, Dr. Muhammad Aslam Khaki,
Advocate, in his personal capacity, has assailed the
observation/recommendation rendered by the Council of
Islamic Ideology (CII) in relation to an accused in criminal
case FIR No.563 of 2025 dated 26.08.2025, registered under
Section 295-C PPC read with Section 11 of the Prevention of
Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 at Police Station Jhelum City,
District Jhelum, wherein one Engr. Mirza Muhammad Ali son
of Muhammad Arshad, resident of District Jhelum, has been
nominated as an accused on the basis of his statement.
2
W.P No.3972-2025
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the
National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA), being the
investigating agency, sought the opinion of the Council of
Islamic Ideology on the matter, as it was uncertain whether
the alleged statement constituted an offence of blasphemy or
otherwise. Pursuant to the NCCIA’s letter dated 12.09.2025
addressed to the Chairman, Council of Islamic Ideology, the
CII rendered its opinion accordingly. The investigation agency
had sought a scholarly opinion regarding a statement made in
a YouTube video, which formed the basis of the criminal case.
Consequently, the Council of Islamic Ideology rendered its
opinion on the principal question, and thereafter the NCCIA
proceeded to charge the accused under Section 295-C PPC
read with the Section 11 of the Prevention of Electronic
Crimes Act, 2016.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner further contends that,
in terms of Articles 229 and 230 of the Constitution of the
Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, the Council of Islamic
Ideology has no jurisdiction to render such an opinion. He
further submits that the constitutional mandate of the
Council of Islamic Ideology is confined to a specific framework
and operates within defined parameters.
4. Notice was also issued to learned Attorney General for
Pakistan under Order XXVII-A CPC for assistance. The
learned Additional Attorney General appeared and, while
3
W.P No.3972-2025
referring Articles 229 and 230 of the Constitution, submitted
that the Council of Islamic Ideology is constitutionally
mandated to make recommendations to the Parliament and
Provincial Assemblies regarding ways and means of enabling
and encouraging Muslims of Pakistan to order their lives,
individually and collectively, in accordance with the principles
and concepts of Islam as enunciated in the Holy Qur’an and
Sunnah. He further argued that the CII may advise the
Parliament, Provincial Assemblies, the President, or the
Governor on any question referred to it concerning a proposed
law, and may also recommend measures for bringing existing
laws into conformity with the injunctions of Islam. It was
emphasized that such recommendations fall within the
jurisdictional framework of the Council of Islamic Ideology
and are to be considered by the competent legislative forums.
5. Arguments heard and record perused.
6. The controversy in the instant matter revolves around
the opinion rendered by the Council of Islamic Ideology on the
request of the NCCIA in relation to FIR No. 563 of 2025. The
NCCIA, while investigating the alleged YouTube statement of
the accused, sought a scholarly opinion from the CII, which
subsequently declared the statement to be blasphemous.
Although the petitioner has no direct nexus with the criminal
case, he has invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of this
Court in public interest, contending that the CII has acted
4
W.P No.3972-2025
beyond its jurisdiction as defined under Articles 229 and 230
of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973.
7. In order to appreciate the controversy in its true
perspective, it is advantageous to reproduce Articles 229 and
230 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan,
1973, which read as under:
“229. Reference by [Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament)], etc., to
Islamic Council.— The President or the Governor of a Province
may, or if [one-fourth] of its total membership so requires, a
House or a Provincial Assembly shall, refer to the Islamic
Council for advice any question as to whether a proposed law
is or is not repugnant to the Injunctions of Islam.
230. Functions of the Islamic Council.— (1) The functions of
the Islamic Council shall be-
(a) to make recommendations to [Majlis-e-Shoora
(Parliament)] and the Provincial Assemblies as to the
ways and means of enabling and encouraging the
Muslims of Pakistan to order their lives individually
and collectively in all respects in accordance with
the principles and concepts of Islam as enunciated
in the Holy Quran and Sunnah;
(b) to advise a House, a Provincial Assembly, the
President or a Governor on any question referred to
the Council as to whether proposed law is or is not
repugnant to the Injunctions of Islam;
(c) to make recommendations as to the measures for
bringing existing laws into conformity with the
Injunctions of Islam and the stages by which such
measures should be brought into effect; and
(d) to compile in a suitable form, for the guidance of
[Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament)] and the Provincial
Assemblies, such Injunctions of Islam as can be given
legislative effect.
5
W.P No.3972-2025
(2) When, under Article 229, a question is referred by a
House, a Provincial Assembly, the President or a Governor to
the Islamic Council, the Council shall, within fifteen days
thereof, inform the House, the Assembly, the President or the
Governor, as the case may be, of the period within which the
Council expects to be able to furnish that advice.
(3) Where a House, a Provincial Assembly, the President
or the Governor, as the case may be, considers that, in the
public interest, the making of the proposed law in relation to
which the question arose should not be postponed until the
advice of the Islamic Council is furnished, the law may be made
before the advice is furnished:
Provided that, where a law is referred for advice to the
Islamic Council and the Council advises that the law is
repugnant to the Injunctions of Islam, the House or, as the case
may be, the Provincial Assembly, the President or the Governor
shall reconsider the law so made.
(4) The Islamic Council shall submit its final report within
seven years of its appointment, and shall submit an annual
interim report. The report, whether interim or final, shall be laid
for discussion before both Houses and each Provincial
Assembly within six months of its receipt, and '[Majlis-e-Shoora
(Parliament)] and the Assembly, after considering the report,
shall enact laws in respect thereof within a period of two years
of the final report[:]
[Provided that the final report in any case shall be considered
within twelve months after it has been laid.]
8. A plain reading of the above referred Articles reveals
that the persons and entities entitled to seek advice from the
CII are:
(i) the President;
(ii) the Governor of a Province; and
(iii) the Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament) or a Provincial
Assembly, subject to the condition that one-fourth of
its total members so require. Furthermore, the advice
6
W.P No.3972-2025
pertains to whether a proposed law or an existing law
is repugnant to the injunctions of Islam.
However, in this case NCCIA does not find mention
anywhere in the constitutional scheme in terms of Articles
229 and 230 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of
Pakistan, 1973, to refer any matter to CII, even though the
status of CII is advisory in nature with limited scope. Such
advisory jurisdiction is, therefore, legislative and policy-
oriented in nature, and does not extend to the examination of
facts of an individual case or the determination of criminal
liability. It is settled law that all the State functionaries must
act strictly within their constitutional mandate, any
assumption of jurisdiction not expressly conferred is ulta
vires as held in PLD 2016 [SC] 808 (Messrs Msutafa Impex
Vs. Government of Pakistan), therefore, when the law
requires a thing to be done in a particular manner, it should
be done in that manner and not otherwise.
9. From the above constitutional scheme, it is evident that
no authority, other than, those specified, can seek advice
from the CII. Moreover, such advice must relate to a proposed
or existing law, and not to the determination of criminal
liability of an individual. In addition to this, the subject
matter being a criminal case does not fall within the
constitutional domain of the CII. The Council of Islamic
Ideology is neither a fact-finding nor an adjudicatory forum,
and its role cannot be extended to pronounce whether a
7
W.P No.3972-2025
particular act of an accused constitutes an offence or not. The
application of penal provisions, including Section 295-C PPC,
necessarily involves appreciation of evidence, assessment of
intent, and determination of facts, which are functions
exclusively vested in the investigating agency and the
competent Court of law, and not in an advisory body
constituted under the Constitution. The NCCIA, if so
required, could have sought independent scholarly opinions
and made them part of the report under Section 173 Cr.P.C.
for consideration by the trial Court. However, the opinion of
the CII, rendered without jurisdiction, cannot be sustained.
10. Furthermore, when examined in the light of Article 10-A
of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, it is
apparent that the principles of due process and fair trial have
been compromised. It is settled law that opinion given by CII
is prejudicing the accused person and violates the right to fair
trial under Article 10-A of the Constitution of Islamic
Republic of Pakistan, 1973, as held in PLD 2015 [SC]
401(District Bar Association Rawalpindi Vs. Federation
of Pakistan).
11. The learned counsel for the CII and its Director (Legal),
while appearing on the previous dates of hearing have placed
several instances where opinions were rendered by the CII
upon requests from various public and private entities.
8
W.P No.3972-2025
However, such past practices cannot override the clear
constitutional limitations imposed by Articles 229 and 230.
12. No doubt, the Council of Islamic Ideology comprises
eminent scholars, and its interpretations of the Qur’an and
Sunnah hold significant intellectual value. However, the issue
at hand concerns the fundamental rights of an individual and
must be adjudicated strictly within the bounds of
constitutional jurisdiction. Therefore, any criminal liability is
the exclusive domain of courts as held in PLD 1999 [SC] 504
(Liaquat Hussain Vs. Federation of Pakistan). The
Constitution does not envisage the Council of Islamic Ideology
as a forum for determining the criminality of individuals, but
as an advisory body for examining the conformity of laws with
the Injunctions of Islam.
13. I have given anxious thought to the Fundamental Rights
enshrined in Chapter I of the Constitution. Article 9
guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or liberty
save in accordance with law; however, the impugned opinion,
in effect, tends to prejudice the rights of the accused and may
curtail his right to life. Similarly, Article 14, which safeguards
the dignity of man, has also been implicated, as the impugned
opinion undermines the constitutional protection afforded to
individuals. Consequently, the impugned opinion is declared
to be in violation of the constitutional framework. It is,
however, observed that, if deemed necessary, the Federal
9
W.P No.3972-2025
Government or the Council of Islamic Ideology may approach
the Parliament for appropriate amendments in Articles 229
and 230 of the Constitution to expand the scope of the CII’s
jurisdiction; until such amendment is made, any exercise
beyond the existing constitutional mandate shall remain
without lawful authority.
14. Accordingly, this Court holds that the opinion rendered
by the Council of Islamic Ideology in FIR No.563 of 2025 is
without lawful authority and jurisdiction, and thus cannot
be given legal effect, therefore, instant writ petition is,
therefore, ALLOWED.
(MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI)
JUDGE
APPROVED FOR REPORTING.
RAMZAN

ORDER-SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Criminal Misc. No.456-B of 2026
Sajjad Amir
Versus
The State & others.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of
order/ order/ parties or counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
19.03.2026 Mr. Zarak Khan, Advocate for petitioner,
Mr. Fahad Khan Tareen, AAG
Shehroz Riaz, SI/CTW/FIA.
INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J: Through the instant
petition, petitioner namely Sajjad Amir prays for post-arrest
bail in FIR No.344, dated 22.12.2025, under Sections 11,20,
26-A of PECA-2016, r/w section 124-A, 109, 34 PPC,
registered at Police Station NCCIA/CCRC, Islamabad
2. Precisely, the allegations set-forth in the FIR are
that pursuant to Enquiry No. RE-2782/2025 conducted by
NCCIA, Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad, it
transpired that the accused persons, namely Muhammad
Hassan, Luqman Khan, Muhammad Abbas, along with an
unidentified person, in active connivance with each other,
allegedly made highly offensive, misleading, and anti-state
statements and also spread fake news against Security
Agencies of Pakistan, during interview with British Vlogger
having YouTube interview with British Vlogger having
YouTube channel namely “Peace Travel”, with malafide
intention and ulterior motives. The accused persons
propagated narratives that align with hostile terrorist groups
and proscribed organizations. Moreover, the accused persons
deliberately glorified the separatist ideologies incite ethnic
hatred, undermine public trust in state institutions and
portray the Armed Forces of Pakistan as responsible for
terrorism, enforced disappearances and collusion with
banned outfit Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).Hence instant
FIR.
3. Arguments heard and perused the record.
2
Crl. Misc. No. 456 of 2026
4. It is well settled that every criminal case is to be
seen in the light of its own peculiar facts and circumstances
and while deciding a bail application, only tentative
assessment of the material collected during the course of
investigation, is permissible and deeper appreciation of the
same is not warranted under the law.
5. The allegation against the petitioner is that he while
being interviewed by a British Vlogger running a YouTube
channel namely „Peace Travels‟, allegedly made highly
offensive, misleading, and anti-state statements against the
State and Security Agencies of Pakistan.
6. Record further reveals that the said video was not
uploaded by the petitioner as the said video was uploaded by
the British Vlogger himself on his own Youtube channel. The
petitioner was not directly nominated in the FIR rather he
was implicated during course of investigation.
7. The main ground urged for grant of bail is that at
the time of alleged offence, the age of the petitioner is less
than 18 years. In support of this contention, learned counsel
produced Form-B issued by the NADRA wherein his date of
birth is written as 29.03.2009, therefore, at the time of
registration of FIR against the petitioner, he is less than 18
years. The Investigating Officer present in the Court also
confirmed that petitioner is juvenile, therefore, apparently he
is a juvenile.
8. Co-accused namely Muhammad Abbas, who was
directly nominated in the FIR, has been granted post arrest
bail by the Learned Trial Court vide order dated 31.12.2025,
therefore, petitioner having the same role is also entitled for
the same relief.
9. The Section 11, 20, 26-A of PECA, 2016 and Section
124-A PPC do not fall within the prohibitory clause of Section
497 Cr.P.C. wherein grant of bail is a rule and refusal is an
exception. This view finds support from the guidance drawn
from the unreported order of the Honourable Supreme Court
of Pakistan dated 20.06.2025 in the case titled “Nazarat v.
3
Crl. Misc. No. 456 of 2026
The State and another” (Criminal Petition No. 824 of
2025), wherein similar principles governing the grant of bail
were reaffirmed.
10. Furthermore, investigation of the case has
already been completed, therefore, further incarceration of the
petitioner, in the attending circumstances, would serve no
useful purpose particularly when he retains no criminal
record.
11. In view of above, instant petition is allowed
and petitioner (Sajjad Amir) is admitted to post arrest bail
subject to his furnishing bail bonds in the sum of
Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees one hundred thousand only), with one
surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned
Trial Court.
12. The observations made hereinabove are tentative in
nature and shall not prejudice the case of either party during
trial.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
*A.R.Ansari*

ORDER SHEET.
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc No.433-B of 2026
Haider Saeed
Vs.
The State, etc.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of
order/ order/ parties or counsel where necessary.
proceedings proceedings
17.03.2026 Syed Ali Bukhari, Hassan Sajjad, Murtaza Hussain Turi, Fida
Hussain Abbasi, Sardar Masroof and Amna Ali, Advocates for
petitioner.
Ms. Shaista Tabassum, AAG.
S.I Muhammad Waseem Sikandar, NCCIA, Islamabad.
Muhammad Asif, J. Through the instant bail petition, the
petitioner/accused, Haider Saeed, seeks post-arrest bail in FIR No.
48/2026 dated 25.02.2026, registered at Police Station NCCIA,
Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad, for offences punishable
under Sections 9, 10, 20 & 26-A of the Prevention of Electronic
Crimes Act (PECA), 2016 (as amended in 2025). Prior to
approaching this Court, the petitioner had moved a bail application
before the learned trial Court, which was declined vide order dated
06.03.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge/MCC,
Islamabad.
2. Succinctly, the facts of the prosecution case, as reflected in the
FIR, are that upon conclusion of enquiry No.RE-492/2026
conducted by NCCIA, it transpired that the petitioner was operating
a social media account on platform “X” (Twitter), through which he
allegedly disseminated provocative, false and misleading
information aimed at inciting public unrest and hatred against State
institutions. It is alleged that on 05.02.2026, the petitioner posted a
tweet whereby he attempted to provoke the general public to block
motorways, highways and inter-provincial routes and to disrupt
supply of electricity, thereby encouraging civil disobedience and
2 | Pa ge
unrest within the State. On the basis of such allegations, the instant
FIR was registered.
3. Learned counsel contends that the petitioner is innocent and has
been falsely implicated in the case. It is argued that the allegations
are vague, general and do not fulfill the essential ingredients of the
offences alleged. It is further contended that no direct or cogent
evidence is available on record to connect the petitioner with the
alleged dissemination of unlawful content. It is also contended that
the case is based on documentary/digital evidence already in
possession of the investigating agency, therefore, physical custody
of the petitioner is no longer required. Lastly, he submits that the
case calls for further inquiry within the meaning of Section 497(2),
Cr.P.C.
4. On the other hand, learned AAG has vehemently opposed the
grant of bail to the petitioner on the ground that sufficient
incriminating material is available on record connecting the
petitioner with the commission of the alleged offence. It is submitted
that the content shared by the petitioner is highly provocative in
nature and is capable of inciting public disorder and unrest, thereby
directly affecting State institutions and public peace.
5. Heard. Record perused.
6. Prima facie, the material collected during investigation,
including the impugned digital content and its attribution to the
petitioner, tentatively indicates his involvement in dissemination of
such information. At this stage, the digital trail and account linkage,
as asserted by the prosecution, are sufficient to connect the petitioner
with the alleged act, without entering into deeper appreciation of
evidence, which is the domain of trial.
7. The offences alleged against the petitioner fall within the
framework of the PECA, 2016, which criminalizes dissemination of
information through an information system with intent to create fear,
panic, or incitement against the State or public. The element of
intent, as contemplated under the Act, is to be examined at trial;
however, at this stage, the nature of the content attributed to the
3 | Pa ge
petitioner prima facie brings the case within the mischief of the
relevant provisions of the law.
8. The contention of learned counsel for the petitioner regarding
further inquiry under Section 497(2), Cr.P.C. has been considered.
However, at this stage, the material available on record does not
appear to suffer from such inherent doubt, conflict or deficiency
which may bring the case within the ambit of further inquiry. The
plea raised requires deeper appreciation of evidence, which cannot
be undertaken at bail stage.
9. In view of the above tentative assessment, there exist reasonable
grounds to believe that the petitioner is involved in the commission
of the alleged offence. Therefore, the instant post-arrest bail petition
stands dismissed.
10. Needless to observe that the observations made hereinabove are
purely tentative in nature and shall not prejudice the case of either
party at the trial.
(Muhammad Asif)
Judge
Shoaib

IN THE ISLAMABADHIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD

The State and another.

proceedings Proceedings
10.03.2026 Mr. Faisal Ajaz Sheikh, Advocate for petitioner.
Mian Muhammad Faisal, DAG
Azhar-ul-Islam father of complainant in person.
Shehroz Riaz SI, FIA, NCCIA with record.
INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J:- Through the instant
Cril. Misc. Petition, petitioner namely Muhammad Awais
seeks post-arrest bail in case FIR No. 08, dated 05.01.2026,
registered under Sections 20, 21, 24 of PECA-2016 r/w
34,109 PPC, at Police Station NCCIA Cyber Crime Reporting
Centre, Islamabad.
2. Precisely, the allegations set-forth in the FIR are that
the petitioner and co accused namely Alyan and Saifi with
active connivance of each other with malafide intention and
ulterior motive, illegally and unathorizedly got access of
personal picture of complainant and her family members.
The co accused namely Saifi managing a WhatsApp group
with the name of “Irum Kajri” as an administrator. The above
mentioned accused persons uploaded the picture of
complainant and her mother Irum along with filthy, vulgar,
and sexually explicit captions in WhatsApp group “Irum
kajri”. The accused person also sent the vulgar and sexually
explicit text/voice massages and GIF images about
complainant and her family members. Hence, the instant
FIR.
3. Arguments Heard. Record Perused.
2
Crl. Misc. No. 266-B of 2026
4. Perusal of record reveals that it is an admitted fact
that the petitioner is husband of the complainant and their
family matrimonial dispute is still subjudice in a Family
Court. Record further reveals that the petitioner has also
filed an application against the complainant’s brother prior
to the complaint filed by the complainant.
5. It is also settled principle of law that the grant of bail
is a rule and refusal is an “exception”, particularly in
offences which do not fall within the prohibitory clause of
Section 497 Cr.P.C. At the bail stage, the Court is not
required to conduct a deeper appreciation of evidence, rather
only a tentative assessment is to be made to determine
whether sufficient grounds exist to further detain the
accused. In the present case, the material available on
record does not justify the continue incarceration of the
petitioner at this stage.
6. The petitioner has been behind bars since his arrest
and investigation is complete; hence, his further
incarceration would serve no fruitful purpose. No previous
conviction or criminal antecedent has been pointed out
against him.
7. At this tentative stage, without touching upon the
merits of the case, the grounds discussed above make the
case of the petitioner one of further inquiry, attracting the
provisions of Section 497(2) Cr.P.C. The petitioner is thus
entitled to the concession of bail.
8. In view of above tentative assessment, petitioner has
made out the case for grant of post-arrest bail at this stage.
Consequently, the instant post-arrest bail petition is allowed
subject to his furnishing of bail bonds in the sum of
Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees one hundred thousand only) with one
3
Crl. Misc. No. 266-B of 2026
surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned
Trial Court.
9. The observations made hereinabove are tentative in
nature and shall have no impact upon merits of the case.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
A.R.Ansari

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl. Misc. No. 242 of 2026
Muhammad Ramzan
Versus
The State, etc.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties
order/ order/ or counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
04.03.2026 Mr. Sajid Ur RehmanMashwani, advocate for
petitioner.
Mian Faisal Irfan, Deputy Attorney General.
Fahad Altaf, SI, FIA-CCRC along with record.
INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J:- Through the instant
Criminal Miscellaneous Petition, the petitioner, namely
Muhammad Ramzan, seeks post-arrest bail in case FIR No.
13, dated 13.01.2026, registered under Section 14 of
Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, read with
Sections 419, 420, 109 and 34 of Pakistan Penal Code, 1860
(PPC), registered at Police Station NCCIA Cyber Crime
Reporting Centre (CCRC), Sub-Circle Islamabad.
2. Precisely, the allegations set-forth in the FIR are
that pursuant to enquiry No. RE-121/2026 conducted by the
NCCIA Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad, the
petitioner along with co-accused persons with malafide
intention, ulterior motives and active connivance of each
other illegally and dishonestly impersonated themselves as
Army officers and consignee of a parcel on WhatsApp. They
transmitted false/misleading information to cheat and
deceive the complainant who works as InDrive driver. The
petitioner further dishonestly/fraudulently induced the
complainant to transfer an amount of PKR 18,000/- on
pretext of payment of consignment into JazzCash, which he
would return to the complainant and when the complainant
delivers him the parcel. However, once the payment was
transferred into the alleged account, the petitioner alongwith
Crl Misc. No. 242-B/2026
-2-
the co-accused cut off contact with the complainant. Hence,
the FIR.
3. Arguments heard. Record perused
4. It is well settled principle that while deciding bail
application, only tentative assessment of the material
collected during the course of investigation is permissible
and deeper appreciation of the same is not warranted under
the law.
5. A tentative assessment of the material available on
record reflects that the allegations against the petitioner are
of serious nature involving impersonation of Army officers
through fake SIMs, WhatsApp accounts and mobile banking
accounts in order to defraud the innocent drivers. The record
further reveals that during the course of enquiry conducted
by NCCIA Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad, various
pieces of digital and banking evidence including transaction
records and technical data were collected, which prima facie,
connect the petitioner with the commission of the alleged
offence.
6. The main contention of learned counsel for the
petitioner is that offences alleged to have been committed by
the petitioner do not fall within the prohibitory clause of
Section 497 Cr.P.C., so he is entitled to the concession of
post arrest bail. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of
"Shameel Ahmad v. The State" (2009 SCMR 174),
graciously held that an accused notwithstanding the
punishment of imprisonment, not falling under the
prohibitory clause, cannot be admitted to bail as a matter of
right overlooking the attending facts and circumstances of
the case. In another case reported as Muhammad Siddique
v. Imtiaz Begum and 2 Others (2002 SCMR 442), the
Hon’ble Supreme Court has held that none can claim bail as
of right in non-bailable offences even though the same does
not fall under the prohibitory clause of section 497 Cr.P.C.
Crl Misc. No. 242-B/2026
-3-
7. The record indicates that the petitioner is involved in
two other criminal cases bearing FIR No. 247 of 2024 and
160 of 2024 of a similar nature, registered under Sections 14
of PECA, 2016 read with Section 419, 420, 468, 471, 109 &
34 P.P.C, at Police Stations FIA Cyber Crime,
Islamabad/Rawalpindi. Given this pattern of repeated
offences, the petitioner's case falls within the ambit of
'EXCEPTION,' wherein the possibility of reoffending upon
release on bail cannot be ruled out.
8. The Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, in the case of
“Muhammad Imran vs. The State and others” (PLD 2021
SC 903), declined bail to an accused on the ground that
multiple criminal cases of the same nature were registered
against him. In paragraph 5 of the said judgment, it was
graciously noted that an accused involved in eight criminal
cases for the same offence was not entitled to bail due to
falling under the 'Exception.'
9. In light of the foregoing, no case for the grant of post-
arrest bail to the petitioner is made out, as his case falls
within the exception to the general rule due to his repeated
involvement in similar offences. Accordingly, the instant
post-arrest bail petition stands dismissed.
10. The observations made herein above are
tentative in nature and shall have no impact upon the trial of
the case in any manner.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
*AR. Ansari/Basit Ali*

IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT

Versus
The State
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of

proceedings Proceedings
02.03.2026 Mr. Muhammad Islam, advocate along with
petitioner on ad-interim bail.
Mr. Fahad Khan Tareen, AAG along with Sheroz
Riaz, S.I, FIA.
INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J:- Through the instant
Crl. Miscellaneous petition, the petitioner seeks pre-arrest
bail in case FIR No. 344 of 2025, dated 22.12.2025,
registered under Sections 11, 20, 26-A of PECA, and
Sections 124-A, 34, and 109 PPC, at Police Station NCCIA
Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad.
2. The facts, in brief, are that pursuant to Enquiry No.
RE-2782/2025 conducted by NCCIA, Cyber Crime
Reporting Centre, Islamabad, it transpired that the
accused persons, namely Muhammad Hassan, Luqman
Khan, Muhammad Abbas, along with an unidentified
person, in active connivance with each other, allegedly
made highly offensive, misleading, and anti-state
statements and also spread fake news against Security
Agencies of Pakistan, during interview with British Vlogger
having YouTube channel namely “Peace Travel”, with
malafide intention and ulterior motives. The accused
persons propagated narratives that align with hostile
terrorist groups and proscribed organizations. Moreover,
the accused persons deliberately glorified the separatist
ideologies incite ethnic hatred, undermine public trust in
state institutions and portray the Armed Forces of
Pakistan as responsible for terrorism, enforced
disappearances and collusion with banned outfit Tehrik-e-
Taliban Pakistan (TTP).Hence instant FIR.
2
Crl. Misc. No.83/2026
3. Arguments heard. Record perused.
4. Perusal of the record reveals that the petitioner,
while being interviewed by a British Vlogger running a
YouTube channel namely „Peace Travels‟, allegedly made
highly offensive, misleading, and anti-state statements
against the State and Security Agencies of Pakistan. The
said interview, which was subsequently uploaded on
YouTube, prima facie, shows that the accused persons
propagated narratives supporting hostile terrorist groups
and proscribed organizations, glorified separatist
ideologies, incited ethnic hatred, and attempted to
undermine public trust in state institutions by portraying
the Armed Forces as responsible for terrorism and
enforced disappearances, and by alleging collusion with
the banned outfit Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The
said act of the petitioner and co-accused shows to
destabilize national security, support terrorist narrative
and intimidated the Government and general public to
create a sense of fear, panic and insecurity.
5. In order to establish a case for the grant of the extra
ordinary concession of pre-arrest bail, the accused has to
establish the essential prerequisite i.e. malafide on part of
the police or complainant aimed at unjustified humiliation
of the accused/petitioner. Prima facie, the petitioner‟s
identity is clear. The Technical analysis report submitted
by NCCIA of Youtube channel namely “Peace Travels”,
reveals the video was uploaded on the said channel, which
is run by a Vlogger from United Kingdom and
streamed/shared online disseminating anti-state
narrative.
6. The record further reveals that the petitioner is
prima facie involved in this case. Furthermore, the
petitioner‟s case does not fall within the ambit of further
inquiry and that the petitioner has failed to establish any
element of malafide on part of the complainant or local
police to falsely implicate the petitioner in this case.
3
Crl. Misc. No.83/2026
7. For what has been discussed above, instant petition
is dismissed and order dated 23.01.2026, whereby the
petitioner was granted ad-interim pre-arrest bail, is hereby
recalled. The observations made hereinabove are tentative
in nature and shall have no impact upon merits of the
case.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
AR.Ansari/Basit Ali

General.
Ms. Misbah Batool, S.I/NCCIA
INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J:- This is second post arrest bail
petition of petitioner namely Irfan Ullah, in case FIR No. 90, dated
24.03.2025, registered under Sections 20, 21, and 24 of PECA read
with Sections 384 and 109 of the Pakistan Penal Code (“PPC”)
registered at Police Station FIA Cyber Crime Centre, Islamabad.
2. Arguments heard. Record perused.
3. On perusal of the record, it appears that the earlier post-
arrest bail application of the petitioner was dismissed by this Court
on merits vide order dated 22.05.2025. The learned counsel for the
petitioner, despite arguing the case at length, has not been able to
point out any fresh ground, material change in circumstances, or
newly surfaced material warranting reconsideration of the matter.
It is a settled principle of law that a subsequent bail application
can only be entertained if filed on fresh grounds or a material
change in circumstances arising after the earlier application has
been dismissed on merits. Mere repetition of grounds already
taken in his first bail application, without any tangible
development or change in circumstances, does not warrant
reconsideration by this Court. Consequently, the instant bail
petition is dismissed.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
AR.Ansari/Basit Ali

proceedings proceedings
24.02.2026 M/s Khalid Mehmood Mughal and Tabassam
Rashid Siddiqui, Advocates for the petitioner.

State.
Misbah Batool, S.I/I.O, NCCIA, Cyber Crime
Reporting Centre along with record.

INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J.- Petitioner Waqas
Ahmed seeks post-arrest bail in case FIR
No.321/2025, dated 21.11.2025, under sections 21
& 24 of PECA, 2016, registered at police station
NCCIA, Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad.
2. The allegation levelled against the petitioner,
as borne out from the contents of the FIR is that he,
with malafide intention and ulterior motive,
illegally and unauthorizedly captured and
disseminated objectionable photographs and videos
of the wife of respondent No. 2 on Facebook for
public viewing, thereby outraging her modesty and
tarnishing her reputation among her family
members, relatives, and the general public. It is
further alleged that the petitioner sent threatening
and blackmailing WhatsApp/text messages from his
mobile numbers to respondent No. 2 and his sons.
3. Arguments heard. Record perused.
2
Crl. Misc.155/2026
4. During the course of arguments, the learned
counsel for the petitioner produced a photocopy of
a compromise allegedly effected between the
petitioner and the wife of respondent No.2 in
relation to a complaint submitted by her at Police
Station Hawalian for initiating proceedings against
the petitioner. The Investigating Officer (I.O.) has
also apprised the Court that, during the course of
investigation, it transpired that the petitioner and
the wife of respondent No. 2 had established
relations prior to the registration of the case. In
these circumstances case of the petitioner is prima
facie one of further inquiry in terms of section
497(2), Cr.P.C.
5. The offences with which the petitioner has
been charged entails maximum punishment upto
seven years and three years, respectively, therefore,
fall outside the ambit of the prohibitory clause of
section 497, Cr.P.C. Grant of bail in such like cases
is a rule and refusal an exception. Reliance is
placed upon the case of Ahmad Shahzad vs. The
state and another, (2023 SCMR 679). The
complete challan has been submitted before the
learned Trial Court on 16.02.2026. The petitioner is
behind bars since 21.11.2025 and his guilt or
innocence shall be determined upon recording of
evidence, therefore, keeping him incarcerated till
the conclusion of the trial would be unwarranted.
6. For the foregoing, the instant petition is
allowed and the petitioner is granted post arrest bail
subject to his furnishing of bail bonds in the sum of
3
Crl. Misc.155/2026
Rs.1,00,000/- with one surety in the like amount to
the satisfaction of the learned Trial Court.
7. Needless to mention, the above observations
are tentative in nature, which shall in no way
prejudice the learned Trial Court.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
R.Anjam.

19.02.2026
Rao Abur Rahim, Advocate for respondent,

Mr. Asif Nawaz, D.D(L), NCCIA.
Arbab Muhammad Tahir, J. By way of listed petition in
terms of section 497 Cr. PC. petitioner Mudassar Ahmed seeks
post arrest bail in FIR No.49, dated 25.02.2023, under section
11 PECA, 2016, read with section 295-A, 295-B, 295-C, 298-A,
109 PPC, P.S. FIA Cyber Crime Reporting Circle, Islamabad on
merits and on statutory ground of delay in conclusion of trial.
2. The petitioner Mudassar Ahmed along-with co-accused Zia
Ali is facing trial in the referred case. The case is at the stage
of recording of evidence. The first post arrest bail petition of the
petitioner, preferred on merits before the trial court, was
dismissed vide order, dated 06.10.2025. The post arrest bail
petition, preferred by co-accused Zia Ali, before this Court
bearing No.700-B/2025, on merits, was dismissed vide order,
dated 12.05.2025. The said co-accused subsequently filed
second petition on statutory ground of delay in conclusion of
trial, which was disposed-of with direction to the trial court to
conclude the trial of the subject case within a period of one
month.
3. Heard the learned counsel for the parties, learned AAG and
perused the record with their able assistance.
2 Crl. Misc. No. 10-B-2026
4. Record reveals that sufficient incriminating material in the
shape of recovery of cell phone and Digital Forensic Analysis
Report is available on record which, prima facie, connects the
petitioner with the commission of the alleged offence, which
entails capital punishment, thus falls within the ambit of the
prohibitory clause of section 497 Cr. PC. The worth of the
statement of the forensic expert cannot be subjected to judicial
scrutiny while adjudicating petition under section 497 Cr. PC. as
it would amount to interfere in the domain of the trial court.
Suffice to observe, petitioner has failed to make out a case for
the grant of post arrest bail on merits.
5. As far as statutory ground of delay in conclusion of trial is
concerned, proper course for the petitioner would be to move
the trial court at the first instance for the relief sought.
6. In view of above, listed Crl. Misc. is dismissed to the
extent of merits, however, petitioner may avail remedy before
trial court on fresh ground i.e. statutory ground of delay in
conclusion of trial, if so advised. The observations ibid, shall
have no impact upon merits and case of either side before the
trial court.
7. Copy of this order shall be sent to the learned Deputy
Attorney General, Prosecutor General ICT with direction to
ensure presence of all the prosecution witnesses before the trial
court on the date(s) fixed. The trial court shall make every
endeavor to conclude the trial at the earliest by keeping it on
fast track. It is expected that learned counsel for the parties
shall extend full cooperation with the trial court for achieving the
task.

ORDER SHEET.
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc. No.157 of 2026
Ali Hamza
Versus
The State & another
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of
order/ order/ parties or counsel where necessary.
proceedings proceedings
17.02.2026 Mr. Basharat Ullah Khan, Advocate for the
petitioner.
Sheikh Junaid Nadeem, Advocate for the
complainant.
Mian Muhammad Faisal Irfan, Deputy Attorney-
General
Shehroz Riaz, Sub-Inspector, CCRC, FIA.
INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J.: Through the instant Criminal
Miscellaneous Petition, petitioner (Ali Hamza) prays for post-
arrest bail in case FIR No.338, dated 15.12.2025, under Sections
13, 14 of PECA-2016, r/w sections 419, 420, 468, 471, 34, and
109 of PPC, registered at Police Station NCCIA Cyber Crime
Reporting Centre Islamabad.
2. Facts of the case as per the FIR are that “Consequent upon
enquiry No. E-2723/2025, it transpired that the accused persons,
namely Tahir s/o Muhammad Safdar and Ali Hamza s/o
Muhammad Bashir, in connivance with each other, allegedly
impersonated themselves as genuine sellers of a Toyota vehicle
advertised on the social media platform “Pak Wheels” and
contacted the complainant, Mr. Rizwan Ur Rehman Khan. The
complainant, intending to purchase the vehicle, requested
issuance of a banker’s cheque amounting to Rs. 7,631,000/- in
favour of Toyota Cantt Motors from Bank Al Habib Limited.
Although the original banker’s cheque was not delivered to the
accused, its digital image was shared through WhatsApp. It is
alleged that the accused, by misuse of electronic communication
and manipulation of financial instrument data, fraudulently
altered another banker’s cheque originally issued for Rs. 1,000/-
and incorporated the particulars of the genuine cheque. The
tampered cheque was thereafter presented through inward
clearing and was dishonestly encashed, causing wrongful loss to
the bank and unlawful gain to the accused. During enquiry
2
Crl. Misc. No.157 of 2026
conducted by NCCIA, relevant banking and electronic record was
collected which, prima facie, connects the accused persons with
the commission of offences punishable under Sections 13 and 14
of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, read with
Sections 419, 420, 468, 471, 34 and 109 PPC. Hence, this FIR.
3. Arguments Heard. Record Perused.
4. Perusal of the record reflects that the petitioner is
nominated in the FIR with a specific role and the electronic and
banking evidence collected prima facie establishes his
involvement in impersonation, electronic forgery and fraudulent
encashment of a banker’s cheque amounting to Rs. 7,631,000/-.
The allegations pertain to a cyber financial fraud committed
through misuse of electronic communication systems.
5. The offences involve serious economic crime affecting
financial institutions and public confidence in electronic banking
systems. Moreover, no malice or mala fide is attributed to the
complainant that the petitioner is falsely implicated. Although the
offences under afore-mentioned sections do not fall within
prohibitory clause of section 497 Cr.P.C. but this principle is not
absolute, rather it depends upon the facts and circumstances of
each case. Reliance is placed on Malik Muhammad Tahir v. The
State and another (2022 SCMR 2040).
6. The nature and gravity of the offence, the manner in which
the alleged fraud has been committed, and the prima facie,
incriminating material available on record do not entitle the
petitioner to the concession of post-arrest bail at this stage.
7. In view of above, petitioner has failed to make out the case
for grant of post-arrest bail at this stage. Consequently, the
instant post-arrest bail petition is dismissed.
8. The observations made hereinabove are tentative in nature
and shall not prejudice the case of either party during trial.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
*A.R.Ansari*

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc. No.114-B/2025
Noman Ali
Versus
The State, etc.
S. No. of order/ Date of order/ Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or counsel
proceedings Proceedings where necessary.
17.02.2026 M/s Naeem Ur Rehman Bhutta and Tariq Mustafa
Mahar, Advocates for the petitioner.
Mr. Sarfraz Rauf, AAG alongwith Sharyar Talat, SI,
NCCIA.
Through this Criminal Miscellaneous Petition, the
petitioner seeks post-arrest bail in case FIR No.273, dated
19.09.2025, offences under section 14 of PECA, 2016, read
with Sections 419/420/387/506/109/34 PPC, P.S.
NCCIA/CCRC, Islamabad.
2. The brief facts, as stated in the instant FIR lodged on
the complaint of Osama Mahsood, are that consequent
upon the conclusion of Enquiry No. RE-1671/2025 of
NCCIA Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad, it
transpired that on 16th of September 2025, the accused (i)
User of Telegram ID having Username @FIA1625 having
Number +923215855453 (ii) Raja Mohsin Zia s/o Zia Ur
Rehman r/o Federal Town. Thanda Pani, House No 6.
Street No 3-B, Islamabad CNIC No. 37403-0546326-9 (iii)
Noman Ali s/o Rehmat All r/o Near Sultana
Foundation, Kashmin Gali, PO Ali Pur, Partal, Tehsil and
District Islamabad CNIC No. 35302-7541244-3 (iv)
Muhammad Waqar s/o Ghulam Mustafa r/o Naye
Abadi, Ali Pur Farash, Islamabad CNIC No 61101-
5154762-9 along with other 04 unknown individuals with
Crl. Misc. No.114-B/2026
2
active connivance of each other, with malafide intentions
& ulterior motives, illegally and unauthorizedly, by
impersonating as FIA Cyber Crime Officials and armed
with weapons, raided the premises i.e. Plot No. 29, Street
No. 40, Sector G-10/4, Islamabad and illegally took
several electronic devices i.e. DVR, 2 Laptops, one LED,
75 Mobile Phone Sets, 07 Passports of different
individuals and PKR 1.5/-Million into their possession
and further blackmailed, harassed and threatened the
administration of office situated at address mentioned
above to cause grievous hurt. Later, the accused persons
contacted the Telegram ID @FIA1625, with the number
+923215855453, and the Telegram ID @TCHRHarry1, and
demanded 150.000/- USDT in lieu of returning the
aforementioned electronic devices and other articles.
Hence, this FIR.
3. At the very outset, learned counsel for the petitioner
submitted that the nomination of the petitioner in the
instant case is based on false, frivolous, concocted and
misrepresented facts; that the fabricated story of the
complainant creates serious doubts in the prosecution
case, being self-created and engineered; that the co-
accused in the instant case has already been granted
post-arrest bail in Criminal Misc. No.2004-B of 2025;
therefore, the case of the present petitioner also calls for
similar treatment under the rule of consistency; that the
complainant has falsely implicated the petitioner with
Crl. Misc. No.114-B/2026
3
mala fide intention to damage his goodwill in society and
to extort money. Moreover, the petitioner has no concern
whatsoever with the allegations as narrated in the FIR;
that the investigation, to the extent of the petitioner, has
already been completed and he is no longer required for
any investigative purpose.
4. Conversely, the learned AAG along with the I.O have
opposed the instant bail application on the ground that
the complainant is the supervisor of the Security
Company that provides security to the Call Centre; that
petitioner is well connected with the alleged crime, who
was in contact with the principal co-accused and such a
CCTV footage is available on record; that principal
accused is still at large and incomplete challan has been
submitted in the Court, therefore, the bail application is
liable to be dismissed.
5. Arguments heard, record perused.
6. Admittedly, there is a delay of about three days in the
lodging of the FIR, for which no reasonable explanation
has been offered. Furthermore, no specific or overt role
has been attributed to the petitioner in the commission of
the alleged offences. The allegations in the FIR are
general in nature and depict the petitioner merely as an
employee of the call centre where the incident allegedly
occurred. The prosecution has failed to demonstrate any
direct participation of the petitioner in impersonation,
extortion, or the act of placing the complainant or other
Crl. Misc. No.114-B/2026
4
employees in fear of death. Mere association with the
place of occurrence or alleged co-accused, without
concrete incriminating material, is insufficient to deny
the concession of bail.
7. It is also significant that no incriminating recovery has
been effected from the possession of the petitioner. The
electronic devices, cash, and other articles allegedly
looted were not recovered from him, nor has any weapon
been attributed to or recovered from his custody. The
prosecution has relied upon CCTV footage and call detail
records; however, a prima facie perusal does not
conclusively establish the petitioner’s involvement. The
appreciation of such electronic evidence requires detailed
examination, evaluation, and correlation, which is neither
desirable nor permissible at the bail stage.
8. Another relevant consideration is that the
investigation to the extent of the present petitioner stands
substantially completed, and the challan has already
been submitted before the learned trial court. The
petitioner is no longer required for custodial
interrogation, and continued incarceration would serve
no useful purpose, particularly when the case against
him rests upon circumstantial and inferential material.
9. Applicability of section 387 PPC is to be determined
at the time of trial, however, remaining alleged offences
also do not fall within prohibitory clause so as to justify
denial of bail as a matter of course. At this stage, the case
Crl. Misc. No.114-B/2026
5
of the petitioner squarely falls within the ambit of further
inquiry as contemplated under section 497(2) Cr.P.C.
10. The co-accused, namely Muhammad Waqar, has
already been granted post-arrest bail by this Court vide
order dated 16.12.2025. The case of the present petitioner
stands on identical footing; thus, the rule of
consistency/parity squarely applies. Since the petitioner
has been attributed the same role as that of the co-
accused who has been granted bail, he is also entitled to
the same concession. Reliance can be placed on these case
laws of the apex court. Mst. ASIYA V/S The STATE and
another, 2023 S C M R 383. SHAHZAD V/S The STATE
and another 2023 S C M R 679. Muhammad Fazal alias
Bodi v. The State (1979 SCMR 9), Muhammad Ajmal v.
The State (2022 SCMR 274), and Muhammad Usman
Shakir v. The State (2021 SCMR 1880).
11. In view of the above, the petitioner/accused is
entitled to post-arrest bail subject to furnishing bail
bonds in the sum of Rs.1,00,000/- (one lac) with one
surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned
Trial Court.
12. The observations made in the preceding paragraphs
are tentative in nature, and the same shall not prejudice
the right of the parties before the learned trial court,
which is to be decided on its own merits.
(KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO)
Crl. Misc. No.114-B/2026
6
JUDGE
Niqab

ORDER SHEET.
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Rev. No.157/2025
Qadir Khan
Vs
The State through FIA
S. No. of Date of
Order with signature of Judge and that of
order/ order/
parties or counsel where necessary.
proceedings proceedings
05 13.02.2026 Ms. Laraib Kanwal, advocate for the
petitioner.
Mian M. Faisal Irfan, learned DAG along with
Fazal Mehmood, S.I., FIA.
Through the instant criminal revision
petition under Sections 435 and 439 Cr.P.C.,
the petitioner, Qadir Khan, calls into question
the validity of order dated 28.10.2025 passed
by the learned Additional Sessions Judge
(West), Islamabad, whereby he was declared
proclaimed offender on account of his non-
appearance and perpetual warrants of arrest
were issued against him.
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner
contended that the impugned order suffers
from non-application of judicial mind and has
been passed without proper appreciation of the
attending facts; that the petitioner had earlier
been admitted to post-arrest bail vide order
dated 20.10.2023 in FIR No.105 dated
16.06.2023 registered under Sections 20, 21
and 24 of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes
2
Crl. Rev. No.157/2025
Act, 2016 read with Section 109 P.P.C. at Police
Station FIA/Cyber Crime Reporting Centre,
Islamabad, and had never misused the
concession of bail; that the petitioner had
proceeded abroad in connection with his
employment and, upon learning about the
dismissal of his application for exemption from
personal appearance under Section 540-A
Cr.P.C. vide order dated 15.07.2025 and
issuance of non-bailable warrants, he promptly
approached this Court through writ petition
No.4364/2025 seeking protective bail to enable
his appearance before the trial Court; that this
Court vide order dated 27.10.2025 granted
protective bail and directed him to appear on
29.10.2025, while restraining his arrest at
Islamabad Airport in the meanwhile; that the
petitioner’s absence from the Court below on
28.10.2025 was neither deliberate nor
contumacious but was occasioned by
circumstances beyond his control.
3. Conversely, learned Deputy Attorney-
General opposed the instant petition by
maintaining that the petitioner had remained
absent from the trial proceedings for a
considerable period, compelling the learned
3
Crl. Rev. No.157/2025
trial Court to decline his request for exemption
and to issue coercive process.
4. Heard. Record perused.
5. The record reflects that vide order dated
20.10.2023 passed by the learned Judge
Prevention of Electronic Crimes Court,
Islamabad, the petitioner was admitted to post-
arrest bail in case FIR No.105 dated
16.06.2023 (supra). Subsequent thereto, the
petitioner proceeded abroad in connection with
his business/employment. During the
pendency of the trial, the petitioner moved an
application under Section 540-A Cr.P.C.
seeking exemption from personal appearance,
which was declined vide order dated
15.07.2025 and non-bailable warrants of arrest
were issued against him. Upon gaining
knowledge of the said proceedings, the
petitioner, prior to his arrival in Pakistan, filed
writ petition No.4364/2025 before this Court
on 23.10.2025 seeking protective bail to enable
his appearance before the competent Court.
Vide order dated 27.10.2025, he was directed
to appear on 29.10.2025 and, in the
meanwhile, restraint was issued against his
arrest at Islamabad Airport upon his arrival.
4
Crl. Rev. No.157/2025
6. The record further reveals that on
28.10.2025, the petitioner was arrested in case
FIR No.1495 registered at Police Station Ratta
Amral, Rawalpindi, despite having been
acquitted twice therein vide orders dated
25.10.2024 and 08.07.2025. Ultimately, he was
again acquitted vide order dated 29.10.2025
passed by the learned Magistrate, Rawalpindi.
Owing to his arrest on 28.10.2025, the
petitioner could not appear before the learned
trial Court on the said date, which resulted in
the passing of the impugned order, declaring
him a proclaimed offender.
7. It is an admitted position that the
petitioner was granted post-arrest bail on
20.10.2023, and there is nothing on record to
suggest that he misused the concession so
extended. The record further reveals that the
petitioner voluntarily approached this
Honourable Court to obtain protective bail prior
to his return to Pakistan. Such conduct, prima
facie, reflects his bona fide intention to submit
to the jurisdiction of the Court rather than to
evade the process of law. An accused cannot be
deprived of his fundamental rights merely on
the ground of alleged abscondence.
5
Crl. Rev. No.157/2025
8. The declaration of an accused as a
proclaimed offender is essentially a coercive
measure, designed to secure his arrest and
ensure his appearance before the Court. It
manifests the resolve of the State to address
deliberate evasion and to uphold the
administration of justice by compelling
submission to due process. However, once an
accused person voluntarily surrenders himself
before a court of law to face trial/proceedings,
then he cannot be disentitled from availing
himself of the remedies provided under the law,
nor can he be deprived of his fundamental right
of access to justice as guaranteed under
Articles 4, 10-A, and 25 of the Constitution.
9. It is a settled principle of law that
abscondence, of itself, does not constitute proof
of guilt, nor can the fundamental right of
access to justice be curtailed merely on account
of alleged abscondence. At best, such conduct
may be considered a relevant circumstance;
however, it cannot take the place of substantive
evidence, nor can it be treated as conclusive of
culpability. Guidance in this regard may be
sought from the law laid down by the
Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan in the
6
Crl. Rev. No.157/2025
case titled “Allah Diwaya and others vs.
Director Education, Quetta and others (PLD
2026 Supreme Court 37)”, wherein the
Hon’ble Supreme Court, while elucidating the
rights of a proclaimed offender, held as
follows:-
“…the right of access to justice cannot be
curtailed merely because a person stands
accused, or has absconded, in another
domain of law. Unless a statute expressly
provides otherwise or the fugitivity
demonstrably obstructs adjudication,
abscondence in a criminal matter cannot
extinguish or suspend independent civil or
service rights.”
Emphasis added.
10. The fact as to the petitioner’s arrest on
28.10.2025 in another case, and his
subsequent acquittal, has not been
controverted. In these circumstances, his
inability to appear before the learned trial
Court on 28.10.2025 stands sufficiently
explained and cannot be construed as
deliberate or contumacious defiance of the
process of law. The declaration of an accused
as a proclaimed offender is a serious coercive
measure intended to secure the attendance of
one who intentionally absconds or evades the
course of justice; such power ought not to be
exercised mechanically where absence is
7
Crl. Rev. No.157/2025
attributable to circumstances beyond the
control of the accused.
11. Consequently, the instant revision
petition is allowed; the impugned order dated
28.10.2025 is set aside; and the matter is
remanded to the learned trial Court to proceed
in accordance with law and to obtain fresh
surety bonds from the petitioner to its
satisfaction. The petitioner shall ensure his
regular attendance before the learned trial
Court, failing which the learned trial Court
shall be at liberty to proceed strictly in
accordance with law.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
Sanaullah*

ORDER SHEET.
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl. Misc. No. 2232-B of 2025
Saqib Shamas
Versus
The State, etc.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or
order/ order/ counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
Mr. Asif Ali Tamboli, Advocate for petitioner,
02.02.2026
Mr. Adil Aziz Qazi and Rao Abur Rahim, Advocates for
respondent,
Mr. Muhammad Sajid Khan Tanoli, DAG,
Mr. Mudasir Shah, Dy: Director and Mr. Asif Nawaz,
D.D(L), NCCIA.
Arbab Muhammad Tahir, J. This is 2nd post-arrest bail
petition by petitioner Saqib Shams for post-arrest bail in FIR
No.102, dated 12.06.2023, under section 11 of the PECA Act
2016, read with sections 295-A, 295-B, 295-C, 298-A and 109
PPC, Police Station Cyber Crime Circle, Islamabad on the
grounds of ‘non-conclusion of trial within the stipulated period’
and ‘statutory ground of delay in conclusion of trial’.
2- Heard the learned counsel for the parties, learned DAG
assisted by DD Law NCCIA and gone through the record with
their able assistance.
3- It is well settled that non-compliance of direction for
conclusion of trial within the stipulated period itself is not
recognized as a ground to claim bail as of right. The guiding
principle on the subject is that accrual of right under third
proviso to section 497(1) Cr. PC is subject to fulfillment of the
conditions mentioned therein. Moreover, while calculating the
quantum of delay attributable to an accused, the court is
required to consider whether or not the progress and conclusion
2 Crl. Misc. No. 2232-B-2025
of the trial was in any manner delayed by the act and omission
on the part of the accused. While ascertaining the delay, the
cumulative effect in disposal of the case has to be considered
and its assessment cannot be determined on the basis of
mathematical calculations by excluding those dates for which
adjournments had been sought by the accused or the latter’s
counsel. The main factor for consideration is the attendance of
the witnesses and whether, despite the matter having become
ripe for the recording of evidence, the delay was caused by the
defense. Guidance may be taken from the case of Muhammad
Usman v. The State and another (2024 SCMR 28).
4- Although, it has been pleaded by referring interim orders
of the trial court, particularly order dated 28.11.2025 that the
delay had been on the part of the prosecution/complainant, yet
the fact remains that the observations of the trial court
contained in its subsequent order dated 20.12.2025, whereby
petitioner’s application for post-arrest bail on the same grounds
was dismissed, depicts different story. It was observed that:-
“The contention of petitioner’s counsel that delay in trial was
caused by prosecution does not get supported from order sheet
of the learned trial court annexed with the petition, on
18.12.2024, examination-in-chief of PW-4 was completed and
the request of proxy counsel for accused case was adjourned for
cross-examination upon all the four prosecution witnesses and
case was adjourned for 09.01.2025 but on the said date an
application under section 265-K Cr. PC has been moved by the
accused-petitioner and notice was given to the complainant for
arguments for 21.01.2025. Despite availing 07 consecutive
opportunities from 21.01.2025, learned counsel for accused-
petitioner failed to argue the said application till 05.06.2025
after lapse of about 06 months he has argued the application
under section 265-K Cr. PC and upon dismissal of the said
application vide order dated 12.06.2025, this case was fixed for
16.06.2025 for cross-examination and remaining prosecution
evidence. On 16.06.2025, fresh Vakalatnama of Mr. Hadi Ali
Chattah and Emaan Zainab Mazari Advocate was filed on behalf
of the accused-petitioner and case was adjourned on the
request of both the parties for 20.06.2025. On 20.06.2025,
3 Crl. Misc. No. 2232-B-2025
again learned senior counsel was not present and case was
adjourned for 25.06.2025 for remaining evidence. Thereafter,
the proceedings of this case were adjourned repeatedly either
on the request of leanerd counsel for the accused-petitioner or
due non-availability of prosecution witnesses and after hectic
efforts made by this court on 28.11.2025, partial cross-
examination upon PW-3 was carried out by the learned counsel
for the accused. On 10.12.2025, PW-3 was present but leanerd
counsel for the accused was required to cross-examine this
witness in the present of A.D (Legal), on that day although he
was on official training and case was adjourned. Therefore, it is
not fair to say that delay has been made by the complainant,
and delay was not caused by prosecution rather accused himself
did not opt to cross-examine the witnesses after lapse of about
one year since 09.01.2025 due to non-availability of counsel or
on flimsy ground as well, hence, no ground even on statutory
ground is available for grant of bail in the instant petition and
the bail petition stands dismissed.” Emphasis supplied
5- It is evident from order ibid, that the witness was present,
examination-in-chief was recorded but the defense got
adjourned the case and thereafter filed application under section
265-K Cr. PC and consumed six months to argue the said
application. After that, new defense counsel was engaged and
then again partial cross-examination was conducted upon PW-3.
Despite the fact that the matter was ripe for recording of
evidence, the delay was caused by the defense. Thus, the
petitioner cannot be absolved of the responsibility of causing
delay in conclusion of the trial.
6- In view of above, petitioner has failed to make out a case
for the grant of post-arrest bail on statutory ground of delay in
conclusion of trial, consequently listed petition fails and is
accordingly dismissed. The learned trial court shall make every
endeavor to conclude the trial at the earliest by keeping it on
fast track. It is expected that learned counsel for the parties
shall extend full cooperation with the trial court for achieving the
task.
4 Crl. Misc. No. 2232-B-2025
7- Copy of this order shall be transmitted to the learned
Deputy Attorney-General and the learned Prosecutor General-
ICT to ensure presence of all the prosecution witnesses before
the trial court on the date/s fixed. Copy be also sent to the trial
court for compliance.
8- The observations recorded hereinabove shall have no
impact upon merits or case of either side before the trial court.
(ARBAB MUHAMMAD TAHIR)
JUDGE
Shafqat*/

petition by petitioner Abbas Butter in FIR No.102, dated
12.06.2023, under section 11 of the PECA Act 2016, read with
sections 295-A, 295-B, 295-C, 298-A and 109 PPC, Police
Station Cyber Crime Circle, Islamabad on ‘merits’, as well as

2- Heard the learned counsel for the parties, learned DAG
assisted by DD Law NCCIA and gone through the record with
their able assistance.
3- Perusal of record reveals that cell phone ‘vivo’ along with
two SIMS having Facebook profiles, allegedly used for the
commission of alleged offence, was recovered from the
possession of the petitioner which, prima facie, connects him
with the commission of alleged offence which entails capital
punishment, thus falls within the ambit of prohibitory clause of
section 497 Cr. PC.
2 Crl. Misc. No. 2191-B-2025
4- As far as the grounds i.e. ‘non-conclusion of trial within the
stipulated period’ and ‘statutory ground of delay in conclusion of
trial’ are concerned, the petition and the documents annexed
therewith are silent as to whether the petitioner, at the first
instance, approached the trial court for the relief as was done in

dismissed by the trial court on these grounds vide order dated

miscellaneous is disposed of in terms that the petitioner held not

to ensure presence of all the prosecution witnesses before the
