ORDER SHEET.
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Criminal Revision No. 84 of 2025
Saqib Shams
Versus
The State, etc.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or
order/ order/ counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
Mr. Asif Ali Tamboli, Advocate for petitioner,
02.02.2026
Mr. Adil Aziz Qazi and Rao Abur Rahim, Advocates for
respondent,
Mr. Muhammad Sajid Khan Tanoli, DAG,
Mr. Mudasir Shah, Dy: Director and Mr. Asif Nawaz,
D.D(L), NCCIA.
Arbab Muhammad Tahir, J:Through the listed petition in
terms of Section 435 read with section 439 Cr PC petitioner
namely Saqib Shams impugns order dated 12.06.2025, passed
by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-Presiding Officer,
Prevention of Electronic Crimes Court,West-Islamabad, whereby
application under section 265-K Cr. PC filed by the petitioner for
acquittal in case FIR No.102, dated 12.06.2023, under section
11 of the PECA Act 2016, read with sections 295-A, 295-B,
295-C, 298-A and 109 PPC, Police Station Cyber Crime Circle,
Islamabad, was dismissed by observing as under:-
“After going through the placed record and hearing both the
sides, it appears that charge against the accused-petitioner is
framed on 28.11.2023 and complainant and accused persons
are appearing. As sufficient material was available against the
accused-petitioner, therefore, charge against the accused was
framed and four witnesses have also been examined. At the
current stage of trial, it would be pre-mature to determine that
the charge against the accused is groundless. The matter would
be concluded after recording of evidence and it would be proper
and right course for the court to adopt recording of evidence
and then to decide the matter according to law. No doubt it is
premature stage of adjudging the guilt or innocence of the
accused without going through the evidence and it cannot be
safely said that the accused is innocent and the charge is
groundless. I do not find any substance in the application at this
stage, therefore the same is rejected being devoid of merits.”
2 Crl. Revision No.84-2025
2- Heard the learned counsel for the parties, learned DAG
assisted by DD Law NCCIA and gone through the record with
their able assistance.
3- There is no cavil to the proposition that by enacting
Sections 249-A and 265-K Cr PC the legislature provided power
to acquit an accused at any stage of the case if, after hearing
the Prosecutor and the accused and for reasons to be recorded,
it considers that the charge is groundless or that there is no
probability of the accused being convicted of any offence. But,
acquittal under the said provisions could be made only if there
was no probability of conviction of the accused. However, each
case must be judged on its own special facts and circumstances
and the reasons are to be recorded in support of conclusion that
the charge is groundless or that there is no probability of
accused being convicted. If there is a remote probability of
conviction, then of course the court is not empowered to invoke
the said provisions. Reliance is placed upon ‘State through
Advocate General, Sindh High Court of Karachi v. Raja Abdur Rehman’
(2005 SCMR 1544).
4- In the present case, incriminating material in the shape of
recovery of cell phone and technical analysis report is available
on record on the basis whereof petitioner had already been
indicted to trial which is in progress. The grounds urged warrant
appreciation of evidence collected during the course of evidence
which cannot be appreciated till the time, it is subjected to test
of cross examination. The petitioner shall have every right to
cross-examine the witnesses and produce his defense.
3 Crl. Revision No.84-2025
5- In the case of Bashir Ahmed v. Zafar Ul Islam
(PLD 2004 SC 298), the Supreme Court of Pakistan did not
approve the decision of criminal cases on application under
section 249-A Cr PC, 265-K Cr PC or in terms Section 561-A
Cr PC by observing that usually a criminal case should be
allowed to be disposed of on merits after recording of
prosecution evidence, statement of accused under section 342
Cr PC, under section 340(2) Cr PC, if so desired by the accused
person and hearing the arguments of the counsel for the parties
and that the provisions of Section 249-A, Section 265-K and
Section 561-A of the Cr. PC should not normally be pressed into
service for decision of a criminal case, especially when
apparently there is a probability of conviction after recording
evidence.
6- Suffice to observe, listed petition fails and is accordingly
dismissed. It is, however, clarified that the observations
recorded in the impugned order and hereinabove shall be
construed and restricted to the extent of application under
section 265-K Cr PC and shall have no impact upon merits and
case of either side before the trial court.
(ARBAB MUHAMMAD TAHIR)
JUDGE
Shafqat*/

case_title: Saqib Ali VS The State etc.
before: Honourable Mr. Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani
author: Honourable Mr. Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani
description: Post Arrest Bail in FIR No. 43/2023 dated 14.02.2023 U/s 11 PECA 2016 r/w 295-A, 295-B, 295-C, 298-A, 109 PPC P.S. FIA Cyber Crime Reporting Circle, Islamabad

pdf_data:
ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
Saqib Ali
Versus
The State and another.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or
order/ order/ counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
27.01.2026 Raja Talha Sarfraz, Advocate for petitioner.
Mr. Usman Rasool Ghumman, AAG.
Rao Abdur Raheem, Advocate for complainant.
Mr. Arif Shahbaz Khan, Director Admin, FIA.
Mr. Sarfraz Khattana, Additional Director Legal,
FIA.
Asim Shahjehan, Inspector, CCRC, F.I.A,
Islamabad.
MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI J. Through this
post arrest bail petition, the petitioner has applied for
post-arrest bail in case FIR No.43 of 2023 dated
14.02.2023, registered pursuant to Enquiry No. RE-
174/2023, under Section 11 of the Prevention of
Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, read with Sections 295-A,
295-B, 295-C, 298-A & 109 PPC, registered at FIA
Cyber Crime Reporting Center, Islamabad.
02. Brief facts referred in the instant FIR are that
consequent upon the conclusion of Enquiry No. RE-
174/2023 of FIA Cyber Crime Reporting Center,
Islamabad, it transpired that the accused Asad
Hussain s/o Muhammad Hussain r/o House No.40/2,
Muhallah C-1 Area, Liaquat Abad, Karachi, CNIC
No.42101-2669593-5, user of a Facebook profile
2
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
having URL
https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=100063471
263079 with profile name “Kashif Khan”, with criminal
intentions and ulterior motives, illegally and
unauthorizedly created, developed, uploaded,
transmitted, disseminated as well as publicly projected
and displayed blasphemous contents i.e.
images/pictures in respect of The Almighty Allah, The
Holy Prophet (peace be upon him), the Holy نینموملا تاہما
اھنع یٰ لاعت ہللا یضر, the Holy Quran Majeed and ىضر تیب لِ ہا
،نیعمجا مھیلع ىلاعت هللا by using the said Facebook profile
and by participating with/in different Facebook
profiles and/or groups, and thereby willfully defiled
and outraged religious feelings, belief as well as spirit
of Islam. Furthermore, during the course of enquiry, a
mobile phone set Infinix Smart-6 bearing IMEI-1
No.353575651695805 and IMEI-2
No.353575651695813, along with mobile phone SIM
No.03003724924 and the above-mentioned Facebook
profile, allegedly being used in the commission of the
subject offences, were recovered and taken into
possession by FIA through seizure memos dated
14.02.2023 in the presence of witnesses. After
completion of enquiry, sufficient incriminating
evidence was stated to have come on record against
the accused Saqib Ali for his involvement in the
commission of offences punishable under the above-
3
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
mentioned provisions, and upon permission of the
competent authority, the FIR was registered.
03. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that
the petitioner has falsely been implicated in the
present case and that the allegations, as reflected in
the FIR and record, are primarily founded upon alleged
attribution of electronic devices and a social media
account, which attribution is yet to be established
through legally admissible and tested evidence. It is
contended that the petitioner is behind the bars for a
considerable period of 02 years and 05 months. The
trial has not yet been concluded and till date only two
prosecution witnesses have been examined to the
extent of their examination-in-chief. He submits that
the prosecution evidence is yet to be tested on the
basis of cross-examination, and as such, no conclusive
or adverse inference can safely be drawn against the
petitioner at this stage.
04. Learned counsel for the petitioner further
contends that the petitioner has not been nominated
directly in the FIR, no specific role has been attributed
to him, and there is neither any call data record nor
any confirmation from the Facebook company is
available to connect the petitioner with this alleged
crime, therefore, case of further inquiry emerges on
record. He further argued that the petitioner has filed
this first post-arrest bail petition before this Court on
4
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
the grounds of statutory delay as well as principle of
consistency. It is contended that two co-accused
namely Asad Hussain and Toqeer Ahmed have already
been granted post-arrest bail vide order dated
19.01.2026 passed in Criminal Misc. No.2177-B of
2025 and Criminal Misc. No.2115-B of 2025
respectively, therefore, the petitioner is also entitled to
the concession of bail on the principle of consistency
as petitioner’s role is not distinguishable at this stage.
05. Conversely, learned counsel for the complainant,
AAG and the officials of NCCIA vehemently opposed
the bail application and contend that the petitioner is
involved in the commission of the offence,
incriminating material has been recovered and the
allegations relate to offences of serious and sensitive
nature involving blasphemous content. It is submitted
that sufficient material is available on record to
connect the petitioner with the alleged offence and that
he does not deserve the concession of bail.
06. Arguments heard and record perused.
07. Tentative assessment of the record reflects that
the prosecution case primarily rests upon the alleged
attribution of a Facebook account and recovery of
electronic devices. The bare perusal of record further
reflects that the petitioner has not been nominated
directly in the FIR, nor has been assigned any specific
role in the factual narration contained therein. On
5
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
plain reading of the FIR, it primarily attributes the
commission of offence to a particular Facebook ID,
which is not in the name of the present petitioner, and
even the mobile number allegedly connected with the
said Facebook ID i.e. 0321-3439141 is also not in the
name of the present petitioner. The Investigating
Officer has been confronted as to whether any Call
Data Record (CDR) was collected, even no other
material was placed on record to prima facie connect
the petitioner with the alleged Facebook account. Even
no report is available on record confirming that
Facebook company verified or authenticated that the
present petitioner was the user or operator of the
alleged Facebook account. Though the Investigating
Officer contends that two different Facebook IDs
allegedly used for uploading blasphemous content
were closed by Facebook, however, no documentary
proof in this regard has been placed on record. So far
as the present petitioner is concerned, perusal of the
FIR reflects that his name does not find direct mention
therein, nor is any specific role attributed to him in the
narration of facts. Prima facie petitioner’s implication
appears to have emerged subsequently during the
course of enquiry and investigation. Without
expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, this
aspect prima facie gives rise to a case of further
inquiry within the meaning of Section 497(2) Cr.P.C.
6
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
particularly at the bail stage where only tentative
assessment is permissible.
08. The petitioner has filed this first post-arrest bail
petition before this Court on the grounds of statutory
delay as well as on the principle of consistency. The
two co-accused namely Asad Hussain and Toqeer
Ahmed have already been granted post-arrest bail vide
order dated 19.01.2026 passed in Criminal Misc.
No.2177-B of 2025 and Criminal Misc. No.2115-B of
2025 respectively, therefore, the petitioner is also
entitled to the concession of bail on the principle of
consistency having similar role as alleged to those co-
accused. Moreover, at this stage, the authorship,
control, custody, and exclusive use of the alleged
social media account, as well as its connection with
the present petitioner, are matters requiring strict
proof during trial through reliable, confidence-
inspiring, and tested which could not be conclusively
determined at the bail stage.
09. It is also evident from the record that the trial
has commenced and only two prosecution witnesses
have been examined to the extent of their examination-
in-chief and their statement have not been subjected
to cross-examination so far, as such, the prosecution
evidence remains untested.
10. Bird’s eye view of the order sheet further reflects
that despite the passage of a substantial period of 02
7
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
years and 05 months from the date of arrest of the
petitioner i.e. 21.08.2023, the trial has not yet been
concluded. The case has been attended on around 47
hearings, out of which on 16 occasions delay
attributed to the prosecution side and on 13 occasions
to the defence side. The petitioner was apprehended on
21.08.2023, charge was framed on 28.11.2024, and
only two prosecution witnesses have been recorded so
far. Prima facie, the delay in recording of prosecution
evidence is not attributable to the petitioner. In this
context, reference may be made to the law laid down
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in 2024
SCMR 28 (Muhammad Usman vs. The State),
wherein it has been held that the right of an accused
to seek bail on statutory grounds cannot be defeated
except in the circumstances expressly provided under
the third and fourth provisos to Section 497(1) Cr.P.C.
11. It has further been held that while calculating
delay, the Court is required to consider the overall
progress of the trial, the attendance of witnesses, and
whether the trial could reasonably have been
concluded but for reasons not attributable to the
accused. Mere framing of charge or partial recording of
prosecution evidence does not defeat the statutory
right of bail.
12. The recording of statements of prosecution
witnesses, without completion of cross-examination,
8
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
also does not defeat the statutory right to bail. It is
settled principle of law that while deciding a bail
application before conclusion of trial, only a tentative
assessment of the material available on record is to be
made, and it is not permissible to undertake a deeper
appreciation of evidence in a manner that might
prejudice either party. Reliance in this regard may be
placed on 2021 SCMR 111 (Imtiaz vs. Azam Khan)
and 2020 SCMR 937 (Bilal Khan vs. The State). It is
also settled that the heinousness of the offence alone
is not sufficient to deny the concession of bail. The
ultimate conviction and incarceration of a guilty
person can repair the wrong caused by a mistaken
grant of bail, however, no satisfactory reparation can
be offered to an accused for unjustified incarceration if
he is ultimately acquitted. Reliance is placed on PLD
1972 [SC] 81 (Manzoor Ahmed vs. The State) and
2016 SCMR 18 (Zaigham Ashraf vs. The State).
13. In the above circumstances, where the accused
remained incarcerated for a substantial period of more
than 02 years and 05 months, the prosecution failed
to ensure presence of witnesses and prosecuting
officers, the continued detention of the petitioners
would amount to punitive incarceration prior to
determination of guilt, which is neither sanctioned by
law nor permissible under settled principles governing
grant of bail.
9
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
14. Keeping in view the entire facts and
circumstances of the case, the nature of allegations,
the stage of trial, the fact that prosecution evidence
has not yet been tested on the basis of cross-
examination, the applicability of the principle of
consistency, and the lapse of statutory period without
conclusion of trial, this Court is of the considered
opinion that the petitioner has made out a case for
grant of post-arrest bail.
15. For what has been discussed above, the instant
post-arrest bail application is ALLOWED, and the
petitioner is admitted to post-arrest bail subject to
furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs.200,000/- with
one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the
learned Trial Court.
16. Before parting with this order, it is observed that
on more than three occasions the prosecutor remained
absent and the learned Trial Court adjourned the
matter. Such practice is deprecated. The Court shall
not adjourn the matter merely on the ground of
absence of the prosecutor. This Court had called the
Officer not below the rank of Additional Director,
NCCIA, vide order dated 26.01.2026 pursuant there to
Mr. Arif Shahbaz Khan, Director Admin, and Mr.
Sarfaraz Khattana, Additional Director Legal, NCCIA
put appearance before this Court, along with learned
AAG and Investigating Officer, who contended that in
10
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
CCR-FIA Islamabad region only one prosecutor post is
available who has to appear before the Federal Court
as well as the Judicial Magistrates, whereas
approximately 200 cases are usually registered in a
month in the Cyber Crime Wing. Though this
constraint was highlighted, it was emphasized that in
sensitive cases, particularly relating to blasphemy,
where complainant counsel are separately appointed
in majority of the cases, the Trial Court shall proceed
by all means and shall not adjourn the matter on
account of absence of the prosecutor alone.
17. Considering the number of cases vis-à-vis
availability of prosecutor, the Government of Pakistan
as well as the Ministry of Interior are directed to
consider increase of the strength of prosecutors in the
NCCIA after amending the relevant service rules, so
that trials may not suffer due to absence of the
prosecutor and the confidence of the public as well as
the Courts in the criminal justice system is
maintained.
18. Copy of this order be transmitted by the
Registrar of this Court, to the Secretary Interior as well
as the Director General NCCIA for consideration in the
policy domain accordingly. Moreover, learned MIT shall
submit a report after verifying the details of cases
pertaining to the Islamabad Capital Territory of all
those accused who have completed the statutory
11
Crl. Misc. No.64-B-2026
period in jail and whose trials have not yet been
concluded. Similarly, details shall also be provided to
this Court regarding pending criminal appeals in
which the convicts have completed the statutory
period and their appeals have not yet been decided by
this Court or by the Court of Sessions. The report shall
be placed before this Court within a period of 10 days.
The jail authorities shall also be informed accordingly
to collect the relevant data from all prisoners / under-
trial accused whose jail appeals / criminal appeals
have not yet been fixed before this Court. Similarly,
both the District and Sessions Judges of East and
West Division, Islamabad, shall also submit their
progress reports in appeals against convictions along
with the reasons for delay.
(MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI)
JUDGE
A.Waheed/-

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Original No.381 of 2025
Sohrab Barkat
Vs.
Riffat Mukhtar Raja, etc.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or
order/ order/ counsel where necessary.
proceedings proceedings
19.01.2026 Mr. Saad Rasool, Advocate for Petitioner.
Ms. Shaista Tabassum, AAG assisted by Mr. Muhammad
Riaz, A.D (Legal) FIA.
Inspector Waqar, NCCIA Islamabad.
Through the instant contempt petition, the petitioner alleges
deliberate and wilful disobedience of the orders dated 31.10.2025 and
24.11.2025 passed by this Court in W.P. No. 4300/2025 and Criminal
Original No. 357/2025, respectively, whereby the respondents were
directed to remove the petitioner’s name from the Provisional
National Identification List (PNIL) or any other travel restriction list
and to comply with the Court’s directions forthwith.
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that despite
these explicit directions, the petitioner was unlawfully detained at
Islamabad International Airport on 27.11.2025, and that no effective
steps were taken by the respondents to ensure the removal of his
name from the PNIL, constituting contempt of this Court’s orders.
3. Conversely, learned AAG, assisted by learned counsel for
respondent No. 1, has produced the compliance report dated
24.11.2025 and subsequent report dated 05.01.2026 of the Assistant
Director, Analysis and Stop List/IBMS, FIA Headquarters,
Islamabad, which demonstrate that the name of the petitioner was
removed from the PNIL in compliance with the Court’s orders dated
31.10.2025 and 24.11.2025. It is further asserted that the petitioner’s
name was later placed on PNIL upon a fresh recommendation of the
National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) due to his
involvement in FIR No. 179/2025 under sections 9, 10, 20, 26-A of
2 | P age
PECA, 2016 registered at P.S. NCCIA Lahore, which falls within the
administrative competence of NCCIA.
4. Heard. The record demonstrates that the orders of this Court
were duly complied with in letter and spirit. The respondents acted in
accordance with the reports submitted and in compliance with the
directions of this Court. The subsequent placement of the petitioner’s
name on PNIL was not a result of disobedience, but pursuant to a
lawful recommendation of NCCIA, which is the competent authority
in the matter.
5. It is a settled principle that contempt proceedings are to
punish willful disobedience of a judicial order. In the present case,
the respondents have implemented the Court’s orders, and the
petitioner has failed to establish that the respondents acted in a
deliberate or wilful manner contrary to the Court’s directions. The
grievances of the petitioner relate to a matter within the
administrative jurisdiction of NCCIA, for which alternate efficacious
remedies are available.
6. This contempt petition is, therefore, dismissed being devoid
of any merit. However, this order shall not preclude the petitioner
from approaching NCCIA or any other competent authority for
redressal of his grievances regarding the PNIL, if so advised.
(Muhammad Asif)
Judge

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Asad Hussain
Versus
The State and another.
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
Toqeer Ahmad
Versus
The State and another.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or
order/ order/ counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
19.01.2026 Mr. Talha Sarfraz, Advocate for petitioner in
Crl.Misc. 2177-2025.
Mr. Asif Ali Tamboli, Advocate for petitioner in
Crl.misc. 2115-2025.
Mr. Usman Rasool Ghumman, AAG.
Rao Abdur Raheem, Advocate for complainant.
Mr. Ilyas Khan, Inspector, NCCIA CCRC/F.I.A,
Islamabad.
Asim Shahjehan, Inspector, CCRC, F.I.A,
Islamabad.
MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI J. By way of this
common order, I intend to decide both the captioned
petitions arisen out of the same F.I.R.
2. Through these bail petitions, the petitioners
namely Asad Hussain and Toqeer Ahmed have
applied for post-arrest bail in case FIR No.43 of
2023, registered pursuant to Enquiry No. RE-
174/2023, under Section 11 of the Prevention of
Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, read with Sections 295-
2
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
A, 295-B, 295-C, 298-A & 109 PPC, registered at FIA
Cyber Crime Reporting Center, Islamabad.
3. Brief facts referred in the instant FIR are that
consequent upon the conclusion of Enquiry No.
RE-174/2023 of FIA Cyber Crime Reporting Center,
Islamabad, it transpired that the accused Asad
Hussain s/o Muhammad Hussain r/o House
No.40/2, Muhallah C-1 Area, Liaquat Abad,
Karachi, CNIC No.42101-2669593-5, user of
Facebook profile having URL
https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=1000634
71263079 with profile name “Kashif Khan”, with
criminal intentions and ulterior motives, illegally and
unauthorizedly created, developed, uploaded,
transmitted, disseminated as well as publicly
projected and displayed blasphemous contents i.e.
images/pictures in respect of The Almighty Allah,
The Holy Prophet (peace be upon him), the Holy تاہما
اھنع یٰ لاعت ہللا یضر نینموملا, the Holy Quran majeed and
،نیعمجا مھیلع ىلاعت هللا ىضر تیب لِ ہا, by using the said
Facebook profile and by participating with/in
different Facebook profiles and/or groups, and
thereby willfully defiled and outraged religious
feelings, belief as well as spirit of Islam.
Furthermore, during the course of enquiry, a mobile
phone set Infinix Smart-6 bearing IMEI-1
3
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
No.353575651695805 and IMEI-2
No.353575651695813, along with mobile phone SIM
No.03003724924 and the above-mentioned Facebook
profile, allegedly being used in the commission of the
subject offences, were recovered from the accused
and taken into possession by FIA through seizure
memos dated 14-02-2023 in the presence of
witnesses. During investigation involvement of
petitioner Toqeer Ahmed has been surfaced on the
basis of which he has been challaned in this case.
After completion of enquiry, sufficient incriminating
evidence was stated to have come on record against
the accused for his involvement in the commission of
offences punishable under the above-mentioned
provisions, and upon permission of the competent
authority, the FIR was registered.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioners contends that
both petitioners have falsely been implicated in the
present case and that the allegations, as reflected in
the FIR and record, are primarily founded upon
alleged attribution of electronic devices and a social
media account, which attribution is yet to be
established through legally admissible and tested
evidence. It is contended that the petitioners are
behind the bars for a considerable period, the trial
has commenced; however, only two prosecution
4
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
witnesses have been examined to the extent of their
examination-in-chief, and till date no cross-
examination has been conducted. He submits that
the prosecution evidence is yet to be tested on the
basis of cross-examination, and as such, no
conclusive or adverse inference can safely be drawn
against the petitioners at this stage.
5. Learned counsel for petitioner Toqeer Ahmed
further contends that his name has not been
nominated directly in the FIR, nor is any specific role
attributed to him in the factual narration contained
therein. He submits that the FIR, on its plain
reading, primarily attributes the alleged occurrence
to a particular Facebook profile and its alleged user,
whereas the implication of petitioner Toqeer Ahmed
has surfaced subsequently during the course of
enquiry and investigation. He argues that such
subsequent implication, without direct nomination in
the FIR and without independent corroboration
available at this stage, raises a serious question
requiring further inquiry, especially at the bail stage
where the Court is required to make only a tentative
assessment without touching the merits of the case.
6. Learned counsels further submits that the
statutory period prescribed for conclusion of trial
has already lapsed, the delay is not attributable to
5
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
the petitioners, and the petitioners are thus entitled
to the concession of post-arrest bail on statutory
grounds, independently and in addition to bail on
merits.
7. Conversely, learned counsel for the complainant,
AAG and the official of NCCIA, vehemently opposes
the bail applications and contends that the
petitioners are involved in the commission of the
offence, that incriminating material has been
recovered, and that the allegations relate to offences
of serious and sensitive nature involving
blasphemous content. It is submited that sufficient
material is available on record to connect the
petitioners with the alleged offence and that they do
not deserve the concession of bail.
8. Arguments heard and record perused.
9. Tentative assessment of the record reflects that
the prosecution case primarily rests upon the alleged
attribution of a Facebook profile and recovery of
electronic devices. At this stage, the authorship,
control, custody, and exclusive use of the alleged
social media account and electronic devices are
matters requiring strict proof during trial through
reliable, confidence-inspiring, and tested evidence.
Such matters cannot be conclusively determined at
the bail stage.
6
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
10. So far as petitioner Toqeer Ahmed is concerned,
perusal of the FIR reflects that his name does not
find direct mention therein, nor is any specific role
attributed to him in the narration of facts. His
implication appears to have emerged subsequently
during the course of enquiry and investigation.
Without expressing any opinion on the merits of the
case, this aspect prima facie gives rise to a case of
further inquiry within the meaning of Section 497(2)
Cr.P.C. particularly when the prosecution evidence
has not yet been subjected to cross-examination.
11. It is also evident from the record that the trial
has commenced and only two prosecution witnesses
have been examined to the extent of their
examination-in-chief. Their statements have not
been subjected to cross-examination so far, and
therefore, the prosecution evidence remains
untested. At the bail stage, such untested evidence
cannot be treated as conclusive or sufficient to deny
the concession of bail.
12. Perusal of the order sheet further reflects that
despite the passage of a substantial period, the trial
has not been concluded. The case has been attended
on around 47 hearings, out of which on 16 occasions
delay attributed to the prosecution side, on 13
occasions to the defense, whereas on the rest of date
7
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
of hearings delay was caused due to different
reasons. The delay in recording and completion of
prosecution evidence does not appear, prima facie, to
be attributable to any act or omission on the part of
the petitioners. In this context, reference may be
made to the law laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme
Court of Pakistan in 2024 SCMR 28 (Muhammad
Usman vs. The State), wherein it has been held that
the right of an accused to seek bail on statutory
grounds cannot be defeated except in the
circumstances expressly provided under the third
and fourth provisos to Section 497(1) Cr.P.C., and
that once the statutory period has expired without
conclusion of trial, the accused becomes entitled to
bail as of right unless the delay is shown to be
attributable to the accused.
13. A disturbing aspect surfacing from the record
is that despite repeated adjournments and prolonged
incarceration of the accused persons, the learned
Trial Court did not adopt the course of appointing a
defence counsel at state expense to ensure
expeditious conclusion of the trial. This omission
becomes more significant when seen in the context of
the constitutional mandate of fair trial and due
process, particularly where the accused persons
remained unrepresented for a considerable period. In
8
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
such circumstances, the delay occurring during trial
cannot be attributed to the accused, rather it reflects
a systemic lapse affecting their right to have the case
decided within a reasonable time.
14. Perusal of the order sheet further reveals that
during the course of trial, the learned Assistant
Director (Legal) representing the prosecution
remained absent on more than three occasions, and
on as many as eleven dates of hearing, no
prosecution witness appeared before the Trial Court.
Such repeated non-appearance of prosecution
witnesses and absence of the prosecuting officer
reflect lack of seriousness on the part of the
prosecution in pursuing the trial with due diligence.
This conduct further strengthens the conclusion that
the delay in conclusion of the trial is not attributable
to the accused persons.
15. Record further reflects that petitioner Toqeer
Ahmed is behind the bars since 15.02.2023, whereas
petitioner Asad Hussain is incarcerated since
14.02.2023. Thus, both petitioners have suffered
incarceration for a period of three years without
conclusion of the trial. Such prolonged detention,
without final adjudication of guilt and without
effective progress in trial, squarely attracts the
applicability of statutory delay, thereby entitling the
9
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
petitioners to the concession of post-arrest bail on
this ground alone, independent of the merits of the
case.
16. It has further been held that while calculating
delay, the Court is required to consider the overall
progress of the trial, the attendance of witnesses,
and whether the trial could reasonably have been
concluded but for reasons not attributable to the
accused. Mere framing of charge or partial recording
of prosecution evidence does not defeat the statutory
right of bail.
17. The recording of statements of prosecution
witnesses, without completion of cross-examination,
also does not defeat the statutory right to bail,
especially, when court has not put any serious effort
for appointing defense counsel on state expense,
which is an alternate method to deal with such
situation. It is settled principle of law that while
deciding a bail application before conclusion of trial,
only a tentative assessment of the material available
on record is to be made, and it is not permissible to
undertake a deeper appreciation of evidence in a
manner that might prejudice either party. Reliance
in this regard may be placed on 2021 SCMR 111
(Imtiaz vs. Azam Khan) and 2020 SCMR 937 (Bilal
Khan vs. The State). It is also settled that the
10
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
heinousness of the offence alone is not sufficient to
deny the concession of bail, and bail is not to be
refused as a measure of punishment. The purpose of
bail is to secure the attendance of the accused before
the trial Court and not to punish him before
conviction. The ultimate conviction and incarceration
of a guilty person can repair the wrong caused by a
mistaken grant of bail, however, no satisfactory
reparation can be offered to an accused for
unjustified incarceration if he is ultimately
acquitted. Reliance is placed on PLD 1972 SC 81
(Manzoor Ahmed vs. The State) and 2016 SCMR
18 (Zaigham Ashraf vs. The State).
18. In the above circumstances, where the accused
remained incarcerated for a substantial period, were
not effectively represented for a considerable time,
and where the prosecution failed to ensure presence
of witnesses and prosecuting officers, the continued
detention of the petitioners would amount to
punitive incarceration prior to determination of guilt,
which is neither sanctioned by law nor permissible
under settled principles governing grant of bail.
19. Keeping in view the entire facts and
circumstances of the case, the nature of allegations,
the stage of trial, the fact that prosecution evidence
has not yet been tested on the basis of cross-
11
Crl. Misc. No.2177-B-2025
Crl. Misc. No.2115-B-2025
examination, and the lapse of statutory period
without conclusion of trial, this Court is of the
considered opinion that both petitioners have made
out a case for grant of post-arrest bail.
20. For what has been discussed above, the instant
post-arrest bail applications are ALLOWED, and the
petitioners Asad Hussain and Toqeer Ahmed are
admitted to post-arrest bail subject to furnishing bail
bonds in the sum of Rs.200,000/- each with one
surety each in the like amount to the satisfaction of
the learned Trial Court.
(MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI)
JUDGE

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl. Misc. No.2246-B/2025
Syed Anees Ahmed Shah
Versus
The State through Anees Ur Rehman, Technical Assistant, NCCIA, Islamabad
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or
order/ order/ counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
08.01.2026 Mr. Muhammad Nasrullah Malik, Advocate for the
petitioner.
Mr. Sarfraz Rauf, learned Assistant Attorney General,
along with Badar Shahzad Khan, Inspector, NCCIA.
KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO J:- Through this bail
petition, the petitioner seeks post-arrest bail in case FIR
No. 285, dated 3.10.2025, offences under sections 6, 7, 8,
10, 11 of PECA, 2016, read with section 109 PPC, P.S
NCCIA, Cyber Crime Reporting Center, Islamabad.
2. Briefly, the facts of the instant FIR are that, pursuant
to the conclusion of Enquiry No. RE-1515/2025 dated
07.09.2025 conducted by the NCCIA, Cyber Crime
Reporting Centre, Islamabad, it transpired that the
accused, namely Syed Anees Ahmed Shah, with mala
fide intention, unlawfully created, operated, and
managed multiple websites providing unauthorized
access to critical infrastructure information and sensitive
personal data of Pakistani citizens, including names,
CNIC numbers, addresses, mobile numbers, CDRs,
location details, and NADRA records. The enquiry
revealed that the accused operated the website pakdb.
Prov, registered on 10.03.2025 and hosted on Hostinger
Crl. Misc. No. 2246-B of 2025
2
servers located in India, besides several other domains
used for similar illegal purposes. Cyber and IP log
analysis established that the said websites were accessed
and managed by the accused through IP addresses
mentioned in the FIR, using a HUAWEI 5G Outdoor CPE
Max (Model N5368X) device, and the mobile number
0302-3213333 registered in his name. It further transpired
that the accused monetized the illegal activity through
Google AdSense. During the enquiry, sufficient
incriminating digital and documentary evidence surfaced
connecting the accused with the commission of the
offence. Consequently, offences under Sections 6, 7, 8, 10
& 14 of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016,
read with Section 109 PPC, were found to be made out
against the accused, hence the registration of the FIR.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that
the case against the petitioner is false and fabricated; that
the petitioner was arrested on 09.10.2025; that despite
being in custody, no substantial progress has been made
in the trial; that the challan under Section 173 Cr.P.C. has
already been submitted; that the alleged offences do not
fall within the prohibitory clause of Section 497 Cr.P.C.;
that the accused-petitioner is entitled to the concession of
bail; and that there is no incriminating evidence available
against him.
4. Conversely, the learned Assistant Attorney General
submitted that the accused was operating illegal websites
through which he was supplying and selling confidential
Crl. Misc. No. 2246-B of 2025
3
and personal data of Pakistani citizens; that during the
course of investigation, sensitive material, including a
laptop and cell phones, was recovered from his
possession; that the cyber analysis report as well as the
forensic report are against the petitioner; and that the
petitioner is involved in a heinous crime, therefore, his
bail application is liable to be dismissed.
5. Arguments heard, record perused.
6. According to the prosecution, the petitioner is prima
facie involved in the creation, operation, and
management of multiple websites, including
simownerdata.xyz.online, livetrackersimdata.online,
siminformation.pro,simownershipdata.info,simownershi
p.online, and siminformation.net.pk. Through these
platforms, access to highly sensitive and protected data
of Pakistani citizens, such as CNIC particulars, mobile
numbers, call detail records, and NADRA related
information, was allegedly made available to customers
on receipt of monetary consideration. Such data, by its
very nature, forms part of critical national infrastructure
and cannot lawfully be accessed, disclosed, or
transmitted except strictly in accordance with law. The
material collected during the investigation prima facie
indicates that the petitioner monetized these unlawful
activities for illegal gain. The seriousness of the
allegations, coupled with the nature of the offence
disentitles the petitioner from the concession of post-
arrest bail at this juncture.
Crl. Misc. No. 2246-B of 2025
4
7. During the course of investigation, the Investigation
Officer recovered a substantial quantity of digital and
electronic devices from the possession of the petitioner,
including multiple laptops, mobile phones of different
makes and models, storage devices, and peripheral
equipment. The recovery comprises working laptops,
several smartphones bearing different IMEI numbers,
USB storage devices, and monitoring equipment, all of
which were taken into possession through a proper
memo. Prima facie, the nature, number, and variety of
the recovered devices are not consistent with ordinary
personal use and lend support to the prosecution's
version that such devices were utilized for the
commission of the alleged offence. The said recoveries
constitute incriminating material, directly connecting the
petitioner with the commission of the offence.
8. The cyber forensic analysis, coupled with IP-
tracking data, reveals that administrative logins to the
relevant websites repeatedly traced back to the accused's
mobile number, 0302-3213333, duly registered in his
name and operated through a HUAWEI 5G Outdoor CPE
Max (Model N5368X) device. Such digital evidence, on a
prima facie assessment, links the accused with the
establishment, functioning, and supervisory control of
the said unlawful websites.
9. According to the investigation report, the website
identified during the course of investigation was PAKTB-
PRO, registered on 10.03.2025, and hosted on a Hostinger
Crl. Misc. No. 2246-B of 2025
5
server located in India. During the course of arguments,
the learned counsel for the petitioner did not deny any of
the documents collected during the investigation, which
connect the petitioner with the commission of the
offence.
10. The offence under Section 10 of the Prevention of
Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, provides for punishment
which may extend to fourteen years, or with a fine which
may extend to fifty million rupees, or with both. While
deciding a bail application, the maximum prescribed
punishment is to be considered at the bail stage. The
offence as alleged does fall within the prohibitory clause
of section 497 Cr.P.C. Reliance is placed on the case titled
"The State/ANF v. Gul Nawab" (Criminal Petition
No.150-K/2024).
11. Consequently, on the basis of the material available
on the record, the petitioner has failed to make out the
case for post-arrest bail; hence, the bail application of the
petitioner is dismissed.
12. The observations made in the preceding paragraphs
are tentative in nature, and the same shall not prejudice
the right of the parties before the learned trial court,
which is to be decided on its own merits.
(KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO)
JUDGE
Niqab
Crl. Misc. No. 2246-B of 2025

author: Honourable Mr. Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
Umair Saleem
Versus
The State through FIA and another.
S. No. of Date of Order with signature of Judge and that of parties
order/ order/ or counsel where necessary.
proceedings Proceedings
31.12.2025 Mr. Qaiser Mehmood, Advocate for the
petitioner.
Mr. Usman Rasool Ghumman, AAG.
Nemo for complainant.
Mr. Asif Nawaz, Deputy Director NCCIA /
Incharge Anti Blasphemy Unit ICT.
MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI J. Through
this Criminal Miscellaneous, the petitioner,
Umair Slaeem, has prayed for his post-arrest
bail in Case FIR No.12 of 2023 dated 10.01.2023
under Section 11 of the Prevention of Electronic
Crimes Act, 2016 read with Sections 295-A, 295-
B, 295-C, 298-A, and 109 PPC, registered at PS
FIA Cyber Crime Circle, Islamabad.
2. Brief facts, referred in the instant FIR
lodged on the complaint of Abdullah Sultan,
are that the complainant has alleged, based on
material obtained from social media platforms
Facebook and WhatsApp, that some unknown
persons are operating in groups from their
2
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
Facebook account IDs referred as
(https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=10
0076580230671,https://www.facebook.com/u
mair.alisaleem.3, 923020041329, and
923162946070) and are illegally and
unauthorizedly creating, developing, uploading,
and transmitting publicly displayed
blasphemous content, images, and pictures. The
complaint was converted into an FIR, whereby
the present petitioner was nominated by the FIA
and the investigation has been completed.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner
inter alia contends that the petitioner was not
nominated in the original complaint. The
petitioner has been indicted in this case
through supplementary statement, nor any
specific role or description has been assigned
to him. Even I.O did not described any role
played by the petitioner towards the
commission of the offence in the challan
submitted in the court, therefore, case of
further enquiry emerges on record. Learned
counsel for the petitioner contends that the
petitioner is behind the bars since 17.01.2023,
and has spent almost three years and so far,
3
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
the trial has not been concluded due to the
delay caused by the prosecution in this case.
Learned counsel for the petitioner also
contends that principal accused nominated in
this case has been granted post-arrest bail,
therefore, rule of consistency applies in favor of
the petitioner, therefore, he is entitled to be
treated at par with his co-accused.
4. Conversely, learned AAG, as well as
the Investigating Officer, opposed the instant
post-arrest bail application on the ground that
Facebook ID of petitioner with e-mail account
has been used as per forensic report, which
connects the accused / petitioner with
blasphemous material, hence, he is not entitled
for grant of bail. However, complainant of the
case was present before the Court on last date
of hearing i.e. 30.12.2025 and matter was
adjourned for today on his request, but today
neither he nor his counsel has put appearance
before the Court.
5. Arguments heard, record perused.
6. Tentative assessment of record
reflects that the petitioner was not directly
nominated in the complaint filed by the
4
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
complainant Abdullah Sultan, which is evident
from the contents of the complaint, where two
Facebook IDs with two different mobile
numbers have been referred.
7. The seizure memo of the online
account in this FIR, Exhibit PW-1/A, reflects
the Facebook URL:
https://www.facebook.com/libaking12. The
description gives login ID:
mk8141820@gmail.com with password:
Liba0245, which was seized in this case.
However, in another case FIR No. 188 of 2022
PS FIA Cybercrime matter reported with similar
allegations by a complainant, and in that FIR,
the seizure memo also reflects the same ID.
Likewise, a third FIR No. 24 of 2023 lodged by
one Imran Farooq with similar allegations also
reflects the same Facebook ID with the same
login and password. Such an aspect confirms
that the same Facebook account and ID have
been used by three different complainants in
three different FIRs against three different set
of accused persons. Despite that, the FIA
authorities have made a single seizure memo of
the complainant’s Facebook ID, and no
5
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
restriction has been imposed, nor any
explanation rendered by the Investigating
Officer as to how the same Facebook ID has
been used by three different complainants.
Such an aspect, if considered in the context of
W.P. No. 2667 of 2024 filed in the Islamabad
High Court, whereby one Noor Fatima, mother
of an accused, made a request to constitute a
Commission of Inquiry due to suspicion of the
existence of a gang entrapping innocent
citizens in cases of blasphemy with ulterior
motives, improper investigation, and the death
of four accused of blasphemy in prison without
judicial or administrative inquiry, which fact
was duly recorded in the order dated
25.09.2025 passed in Criminal Petition
No.1330-L of 2024 titled “Muhammad Umar
versus The State” by the Supreme Court of
Pakistan, whereby the accused persons were
granted post-arrest bail on this single count,
the petitioner is also entitled for grant of post
arrest bail. As such, all these aspects
cumulatively disclose a factum of further
inquiry in terms of subsection (2) of section
497 Cr.P.C in favour of the petitioner. The
6
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
Investigating Officer conceded before the Court
that till date, the Facebook ID of the
complainant as well as the number have not
been verified, as the same is required to be
verified by Meta, the company which is not in
Pakistan. Moreover, not a single statement
under Section 161 Cr.P.C. was referred in
which the complainant owns the Facebook ID
through which he received any blasphemous
content. In such an aspect, the ground of
further inquiry in terms of Subsection (2) of
Section 497 Cr.P.C. emerges on record.
8. I have also confronted the
Investigating Officer present in Court to
authenticate those blasphemous content
pictures as to whether they are genuine or
doctored, and whether they were created by the
petitioner and transmitted to others. However,
the Investigating Officer was unable to
demonstrate from any record that the pictures
allegedly referred to are the handiwork of the
petitioner. Such an aspect is also a ground of
further inquiry. Besides these aspects, this
Court is of the view, by comparing all the
blasphemous content which is similar in all
7
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
other cases presented before this Court in
different FIRs, that when the Investigating
Officer has conceded that the petitioner is not
the author nor the creator of any blasphemous
content, the primary allegation is required to
be established in the trial court. Learned
counsel for the petitioner also pointed out that
principal accused Muhammad Abdullah Shoaib
has already been granted bail vide order dated
03.11.2025 through Criminal Miscellaneous
No.1809-B-2025, by this Court, hence, rule of
consistency also comes on record.
9. I have also gone through the record
and convinced that the entire case has been
proceeded in violation of Section 156 Cr.P.C.
and Section 196 Cr.P.C., and no record of the
cellular service provider is available, nor the
subscriber of the SIM. All such scenarios
create doubt. Besides this, the petitioner is
behind the bars for three years w.e.f.
17.01.2023, and the trial has not yet been
concluded, whereby, two PWs have been
recorded, though examination in chief of four
PWs has been recorded. In this backdrop, the
petitioner has earned his right of bail both on
8
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
merit, rule of consistency, as well as on
account of statutory delay, in which no lawful
justification has been rendered from the
prosecution side as to why the instant case has
not yet been concluded. Therefore, considering
all these aspects as well as the allegations
contained in this case, a tentative assessment
is made by this Court, as it is not permissible
to go into the details of the evidence in any
manner which might prejudice either party.
However, it is also a settled law that the
heinousness of the offence alone is not
sufficient to deprive the Court of its discretion
to grant bail, which is never refused as
punishment. There is no legal or moral
compulsion to keep a person incarcerated
merely because of the severity of the charge.
Hence, considering the mandate of PLD 1972
[SC] 81 (Manzoor Vs. State) and 2016 SCMR
18 (Zaigham Ashraf Vs. State), instant post-
arrest bail application is ALLOWED, subject to
furnishing bail bonds in the sum of
Rs.200,000/- with one surety in the like amount
to the satisfaction of learned trial court with an
additional amount of Rs.50,000/- to be
9
Crl. Misc. No.2189-B-2025
deposited in the trial court account as surety
to ensure the petitioner’s presence before the
trial court till the conclusion of the trial.
(MOHSIN AKHTAR KAYANI)
JUDGE
A.Waheed/-

ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl. Misc. No. 1960-B of 2025
Bai Xiaoming
Versus
The State, etc.

proceedings Proceedings
22.12.2025 Mr. Zeeshan Riaz Cheema, Advocate for
petitioner.
Mian Muhammad Faisal Irfan, Deputy Attorney
General
Shehroz Riaz S.I./FIA.
Complainant in person.
Inaam Ameen Minhas, J: This is second post arrest
bail petition of petitioner on statutory ground in case FIR. No.
250 dated 20.10.2024, under Section 14 of PECA, 2016 read with
Section 419, 420, 468, 471, 109 & 34 P.P.C, registered at Police
Station F.I.A, Cyber Crime, Islamabad.
2. The subject FIR stood registered on the complaint of
respondent No. 2 namely Haris Ahmed Sheikh on the allegations
that the petitioner Bai Xiaoming alongwith co-accused namely
Shehzada Ayaz Latif, Noman Abid Malik, Tahir Waseem, Husnain
Khan alongwith others with malafide intention and ulterior
motives dishonestly allured the complainant on the pretext of
online investment for Stock Exchange of Pakistan and got
transferred amount of Rs.19,391,000/-.
3. Heard and record perused.
4. Earlier bail application of the petitioner was dismissed
upto the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan on merits. The
Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan while disposing of the bail
application of the petitioner observed that “In view of the request
made by the petitioner’s counsel, the Trial Court is directed to
conclude the trial of the case within a period of two months from the
date of receipt of certified copy of this order.”
Crl Misc. No. 1960-B/2025
-2-
5. Now the petitioner has filed the instant bail application on
the ground that he is in jail for more than one year and since
framing of charge on 03.06.2025, the prosecution has failed to
conclude the trial despite direction of the Hon’ble Supreme Court
of Pakistan to conclude the trial within two months.
6. Perusal of record reveals that after investigation, report in
terms of Section 173 Cr.P.C. was submitted before the Court of
competent jurisdiction on 15.11.2024. Charge was framed
against the petitioner on 03.06.2025 and till 22.10.2025, case was
adjourned for about 30 times. During this, statements of two
witnesses were recorded while examination in chief of PW-3 was
also recorded but cross-examination was not done by the learned
defence counsel. During this, miscellaneous applications i.e.
application of E-Court and application under Section 540 Cr.P.C
were filed by the petitioner. Bare perusal of order sheet reveals
that on some of the dates, learned defence counsel was not
present while on some dates, petitioner was not produced before
the Court due to law and order situation and on some dates,
learned Presiding officer was not available. It is therefore, quite
obvious that the petitioner is also contributory in causing delay in
conclusion of trial.
7. It is also apparent from record that although the
supplementary challan against co-accused was submitted by the
prosecution but the trial could not be concluded despite the
directions issued by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan.
Investigating Officer present in the Court undertakes that all the
remaining prosecution witnesses will be produced before the
Court without any delay on their part.
9. The record indicates that the petitioner was convicted
and sentenced in case FIR No. 247 of 2024 of a similar nature,
registered under Sections 14 of PECA, 2016 read with Section
419, 420, 468, 471, 109 & 34 P.P.C, at Police Stations FIA Cyber
Crime, Islamabad, therefore, the case of the petitioner falls within
the ambit of 'EXCEPTION,'
Crl Misc. No. 1960-B/2025
-3-
10. In light of the foregoing, no case for the grant of post-
arrest bail to the petitioner is made out, as his case falls within
the exception to the general rule due to awarding of conviction
and sentence in similar offences. Accordingly, the instant post-
arrest bail petition stands dismissed.
11 The observations made herein above are tentative in
nature and shall have no impact upon the trial of the case in any
manner.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
JUDGE
*AR. Ansari*

SSForm No: HCJD/C-121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT.
Crl. Misc. No.2033-B/2025
Muhammad Qasim
Versus
The State, etc.
S. No. of order/ Date of order/ Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or counsel
proceedings Proceedings where necessary.
17.12.2025 Rana Shaheen Ahmed, Advocate for the petitioner.
Mr. Sarfraz Rauf, Assistant Attorney General.
Zubair, SI/I.O, FIA.
KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO J:- Through this Criminal
Miscellaneous Petition, the petitioner seeks post-arrest
bail in case FIR No.254/2025 dated 09.09.2025, offence
under sections 20, 21 & 24 PECA 2016 r/w 109 PPC P.S.
NCCIA, Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Islamabad.
2. The brief facts stated in the FIR are that the accused,
with malafide intention and ulterior motives, illegally and
without authorization captured/recorded and kept in his
possession sexually explicit pictures and videos of the
victim/complainant. It is further alleged that he publicly
uploaded, transmitted, and communicated the
complainant’s sexually explicit pictures/videos through
an Instagram ID (URL mentioned in the FIR) and from his
WhatsApp account (number mentioned in the FIR) to the
WhatsApp account of the complainant’s ex-husband. As a
result, the modesty and privacy of the complainant were
disgraced and destroyed among her family members and
relatives, hence the registration of the FIR.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the
petitioner is innocent and has falsely been implicated in
the instant case; that victim Muqadas Bibi is legally
2
Crl. Misc. No.2033-B/2025
wedded wife of the petitioner; that he cannot think to
upload the nude pictures of the complainant; that video
which was uploaded in different WhatsApp group has
not been recorded by the petitioner; that petitioner was
arrested on 17.09.2025 and challan has been submitted;
that petitioner is no more required for further
investigation, case of the petitioner falls within the ambit
of further inquiry, request for post-arrest bail.
4. Conversely, learned AAG opposed the bail
application and submits that the petitioner is nominated
in the FIR with a specific role of uploading nude videos
of the complainant; that the mobile recovered from the
possession of the petitioner, sent to a forensic expert,
and received a positive report; therefore, the petitioner
is not entitled to the concession of post-arrest bail.
5. Arguments heard, record perused.
6. The petitioner stands nominated in the FIR with a
specific, direct, and active role of unlawfully capturing,
retaining, and disseminating sexually explicit pictures and
videos of the complainant. The allegations are not vague
or general in nature; rather, they are supported by
tangible digital evidence. The record reflects that during
the course of the investigation, the petitioner was arrested,
and a mobile phone was recovered from his possession
through a duly prepared recovery memo. The said device
was sent for forensic examination, and the forensic report
has categorically confirmed that sexually explicit content
pertaining to the complainant was transmitted from the
3
Crl. Misc. No.2033-B/2025
WhatsApp number attributed to the petitioner to more
than thirty recipients. The forensic analysis further
establishes that some of the explicit videos were also sent
directly to the complainant herself, thereby reinforcing the
prosecution’s stance regarding the petitioner’s active
involvement. Moreover, the forensic expert has confirmed
the genuineness and integrity of the digital content,
negating any possibility of fabrication or tampering at this
stage. The presence of the petitioner alongside the
complainant in the impugned videos further strengthens
the prosecution’s case and prima facie connects the
petitioner with the commission of the alleged offences.
7. The contention raised by learned counsel for the
petitioner that the petitioner’s mobile phone was misused
by some unknown person is wholly unsubstantiated and
appears to be an afterthought. Not only was this plea not
raised at the earliest opportunity, but no material
whatsoever has been brought on record to lend credence
to such an assertion. During the investigation, the
petitioner neither lodged any complaint regarding the
alleged misuse of his device nor disclosed any
circumstance suggesting loss of control over the same. In
bail proceedings, mere assertions, without supporting
material, do not suffice to dislodge a strong prima facie
case established through forensic evidence.
8. Equally unconvincing is the plea that the complainant
is the legally wedded wife of the petitioner. Even if
4
Crl. Misc. No.2033-B/2025
assumed for the sake of argument, such a relationship
does not confer any lawful justification upon the
petitioner to record, retain, or publicly disseminate
sexually explicit content. On the contrary, such conduct
aggravates the offence and reflects a higher degree of
moral and legal culpability. The argument advanced by
learned counsel is thus not only legally untenable but also
contrary to basic principles of privacy and dignity
protected under the law.
9. Such acts also have a devastating and enduring
impact on the life of the victim herself, extending far
beyond the immediate commission of the offence. The
non-consensual circulation of intimate images and videos
inflicts profound psychological harm, including anxiety,
depression, loss of self-worth, and a persistent fear of
social exposure. The stigma attached to such incidents can
adversely affect the victim’s prospects of education,
employment, marriage, and social integration, thereby
impairing her ability to lead a normal and dignified life.
The constant apprehension that the explicit material may
resurface or be further disseminated perpetuates
emotional distress and robs the victim of peace of mind
and personal autonomy. Such victimization amounts to a
continuing wrong, the effects of which do not cease with
the initial act but linger as a lifelong burden, underscoring
the gravity of the offence and the compelling need for a
firm judicial response to deter similar conduct and to
protect the fundamental right to dignity and privacy.
5
Crl. Misc. No.2033-B/2025
10. The ripple effects of such offences extend well beyond
the individual and deeply affect Pakistani society as a
whole. Acts involving the non-consensual creation and
dissemination of sexually explicit material corrode the
collective moral fabric and sense of social security,
particularly in a society where honour, modesty, and
personal reputation are foundational social values. Such
conduct fuels fear and mistrust, especially among women
and young persons, discouraging their meaningful
participation in social, educational, and professional
spheres. It reinforces a climate of digital insecurity, where
modern communication platforms become tools of
exploitation rather than empowerment. Moreover, the
normalization or trivialization of such crimes contributes
to the erosion of ethical boundaries, weakens respect for
the law, and emboldens perpetrators who perceive digital
abuse as a low-risk activity. The cumulative effect is a
society burdened with increased incidents of cyber
exploitation, silencing of victims due to fear of stigma,
and a gradual breakdown of confidence in legal and social
protections. These offences, therefore, do not remain
confined to a private wrong but constitute a serious social
menace, undermining public morality, social harmony,
and the constitutional promise of dignity and safety for all
citizens.
6
Crl. Misc. No.2033-B/2025
11. In light of the above discussion, the present case does
not fall within the ambit of further inquiry as envisaged
under section 497(2) Cr.PC. The allegations are supported
by direct digital evidence, corroborated by forensic
analysis, and establish reasonable grounds to believe that
the petitioner has committed the alleged offences. The
severity of the allegations, the nature of the evidence, and
the manner in which the offence is alleged to have been
committed disentitle the petitioner from the concession of
post-arrest bail.
12. In view of the above, the instant petition is not made
out, and the same is hereby dismissed. It is clarified that
the observations made hereinabove are tentative in nature
and shall not prejudice the Trial, which shall be decided
on its own merits.
(KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO)
JUDGE
Niqab

Muhammad Waqar s/o Ghulam Mustafa r/o Naye
Crl. Misc. No.2004-B/2025
2
Abadi, Ali Pur Farash, Islamabad CNIC No 61101-
5154762-9 along with other 04 unknown individuals with
active connivance of each other, with malafide intentions
& ulterior motives, illegally and unauthorizedly, by

with weapons, raided the premises i.e. Plot No. 29, Street
No. 40, Sector G-10/4, Islamabad and illegally took
several electronic devices i.e. DVR, 2 Laptops, one LED,
75 Mobile Phone Sets, 07 Passports of different
individuals and PKR 1.5/-Million into their possession
and further blackmailed, harassed and threatened the
administration of office situated at address mentioned
above to cause grievous hurt. Later, the accused persons
contacted the Telegram ID @FIA1625, with the number
+923215855453, and the Telegram ID @TCHRHarry1, and
demanded 150.000/- USDT in lieu of returning the
aforementioned electronic devices and other articles.
Hence, this FIR.
3. At the very outset, the learned counsel for the
petitioner submits that the petitioner has falsely been
involved in this case; that there delay of three days in the
registration of FIR for which no reasonable explanation
has been given; that date and time of occurrence is
unknown; that the petitioner is employee of the same
Call Centre; that complainant has not disclosed the
telegram I.D used by the present petitioner; that nothing
has been recovered from the petitioner; that investigation
to the extent of petitioner has been completed, he is no
Crl. Misc. No.2004-B/2025
3
more required for the purposes of investigation; that
challan has been submitted before the trial court; that
section 387 PPC does not attracts in this case and the
allegation of personation falls u/s 170 PPC. Learned
counsel has relied upon the case laws reported as 2011
MLD 865, 2019 SCMR 1914, 2020 PCrLJ Note 155, 2023
PCrLJ 114.
4. Conversely, the learned AAG along with the
complainant and I.O have opposed the instant bail
application on the ground that the complainant is the
supervisor of the Security Company that provides
security to the Call Centre; that petitioner is well
connected with the alleged crime, who was in contact
with the principal co-accused and such a CCTV footage is
available on record; that principal accused is still at large
and incomplete challan has been submitted in the Court,
therefore, the bail application is liable to be dismissed.
5. Arguments heard, record perused.
6. Admittedly, there is a delay of about three days in the
lodging of the FIR, for which no reasonable explanation
has been offered. Furthermore, no specific or overt role
has been attributed to the petitioner in the commission of
the alleged offences. The allegations in the FIR are
general in nature and depict the petitioner merely as an
employee of the call centre where the incident allegedly
occurred. The prosecution has failed to demonstrate any
direct participation of the petitioner in impersonation,
extortion, or the act of placing the complainant or other
Crl. Misc. No.2004-B/2025
4
employees in fear of death. Mere association with the
place of occurrence or alleged co-accused, without
concrete incriminating material, is insufficient to deny
the concession of bail.
7. It is also significant that no incriminating recovery has
been effected from the possession of the petitioner. The
electronic devices, cash, and other articles allegedly
looted were not recovered from him, nor has any weapon
been attributed to or recovered from his custody. The
prosecution has relied upon CCTV footage and call detail
records; however, a prima facie perusal does not
conclusively establish the petitioner’s involvement. The
appreciation of such electronic evidence requires detailed
examination, evaluation, and correlation, which is neither
desirable nor permissible at the bail stage.
8. Another relevant consideration is that the
investigation to the extent of the present petitioner stands
substantially completed, and the challan has already
been submitted before the learned trial court. The
petitioner is no longer required for custodial
interrogation, and continued incarceration would serve
no useful purpose, particularly when the case against
him rests upon circumstantial and inferential material.
9. Applicability of section 387 PPC is to be determined
at the time of trial, however, remaining alleged offences
also do not fall within prohibitory clause so as to justify
denial of bail as a matter of course. At this stage, the case
Crl. Misc. No.2004-B/2025
5
of the petitioner squarely falls within the ambit of further
inquiry as contemplated under section 497(2) Cr.P.C.
10. In view of the above, the instant petition is allowed,
and the petitioner is enlarged on bail after arrest in the
aforementioned case subject to furnishing bail bonds in
the sum of Rs.100,000/- with one surety in the like
amount to the satisfaction of the learned Trial Court. It is
clarified that the observations made above are tentative
and shall not prejudice the trial, which is to be decided
on its own merits.
(KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO)
JUDGE
Niqab

ORDER SHEET

Versus
Mr. M. Nadir Khan, Sub-Inspector, Cyber Crime Investigation Agency/Cyber Crime

proceedings Proceedings
09.12.2025 Mr. Hadi Ali Chattha and Ms. Imaan Zainab Hazir,
Advocates for the petitioner.

alongwith Sarfraz Ahmed Khattak, Director (law),
NCCIA and Badar Shahzad, Inspector/I.O, NCCIA.
Mr. Sarwar Shahid, Head External Agents, NBP.
Through this Criminal Original under Article 204 of
the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan,
1973, read with 3 & 4 of the Contempt of Court
Ordinance, 2003, the petitioner seeks initiation of
contempt proceedings against the contemnors/
respondents No. 1 to 4 on the ground that order passed
by this court on 04.09.2025 in writ petition No.
2446/2025, has not been obeyed.
2. Learned counsel for the applicant submits that the
order passed by this court in the aforesaid writ petition,
whereby a conceding statement was given by the
respondents to de-freeze the accounts of the petitioner,
has been violated intentionally, deliberately, and
knowingly. Counsel submits that on 24.09.2025, the
account of the petitioner was opened, and she withdrew
Rs.50,000/-; thereafter, her account was again frozen by
respondent No.4 on the direction of respondents No. 1
2
Crl. Original No. 367/2025
to 3 without lawful justification. Counsel submits that
the petitioner is a senior citizen and the account in
question is her pension account. Learned counsel for the
petitioner further submitted that cheque No.74875568
dated 07.11.2025 was returned with the remarks
restricted account.
4. The respondents appeared in person and submitted
that no defiance of the court’s order was committed and
that the account has not been blocked. The respondent
submitted the account statement of the petitioner, which
was taken on the record.
5. I have heard the arguments of learned counsels for
the parties and meticulously perused the record with their
able assistance.
6. In compliance with the directions contained in the
order dated 02.12.2025, the Contemnor appeared before
this court, tendered an unconditional apology, and
submitted that they have not committed any defiance of
the court’s order. It was further stated that the petitioner’s
account was neither blocked by any written order nor is it
required in any pending inquiry. The petitioner’s account
had already been unblocked/unfrozen on 15.07.2025 and
has remained active since then.
7. Contemnor/respondent No.4 has also appeared and
produced the petitioner’s account statement. A perusal of
the same reflects that the petitioner has undertaken
twenty-three separate transactions. For clarity and proper
appreciation, the statement discloses transaction dates,
3
Crl. Original No. 367/2025
including inter alia, 30.06.2025, 01.08.2025, 01.09.2025,
24.09.2025, 02.10.2025, 03.11.2025, and 01.12.2025.
6. In view of the above, no case of contempt is made out
against the respondents. Accordingly, the instant contempt
petition is dismissed.
(KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO)
JUDGE
Niqab
